# EstreGenesis Changelog

Each tier (Master / Lite / Compact) has its own version. Master is the authoritative evolution track; Lite and Compact are derived regularly from Master but may lag by a release.

This file is the **changelog SSoT** — each seed file keeps only a compact header metadata line with tier, language, current version, counterpart, and a pointer back to this `CHANGELOG.md`, not the target project's README. When you upgrade a project using Migration B, the agent uses the seed header version marker plus this changelog to compute the delta.

**Language**: **English** (below) · [한국어](#한국어)

## Changelog (English)

- **v2.6.93** (2026-08-08) — the operator asked why selecting the local group addressed a channel belonging to an upstream peer. Two functions were answering the same question — who belongs to this group — and answering it differently: the tab renderer excluded hidden channels and applied the operator's saved tab order, while the send-target resolver did neither and took the first member in map-insertion order. The leftmost tab on screen and the channel a message would actually reach could therefore diverge, and a hidden channel could become the group representative, which means addressing a channel that is not on screen at all. The resolver now reads the rendered group, so the representative is the first visible tab by construction rather than by coincidence, and all seven groups were measured to agree afterwards. Nothing had left the board — the upstream channels showed no traffic in the preceding six hours, so a wrong indicator was caught before it became a wrong send, which is the only reason this is a display defect and not a disclosure. One thing was deliberately left alone: an unrecognised role still falls back to local, and the line that does it now says so. Removing that fallback would drop those channels out of every group and off the screen, and absence is a worse failure than miscategorisation, because a channel nobody can see is a channel nobody can correct. The mitigation is that the representative is now what the operator sees, so a miscategorised channel is visible in the place it was wrongly filed rather than silently selected behind the interface.

- **v2.6.92** (2026-08-07) — Constellation v2.4.151 — the login screen was gating the overlay and nothing else. Measured with one account created and `loginRequired:true`: a cookieless request to the board-state endpoint returned the entire board — planned, done, decisions, projects. No developer tools were needed to see it; `curl` was enough. The visual layer was covering data that was never being withheld, which is the failure mode where a security control reports as present because it is *visible*. Both read paths are now gated on an authenticated operator session, and the same gate covers the streaming endpoint, because closing the request path while leaving the stream open would have been recorded as a fix while the data kept flowing. The websocket side door is closed with a discriminator the file already contained rather than a new one: browsers send `Origin` and library clients do not, a distinction this specification had already relied on to close cross-site websocket hijacking — so a browser-class upgrade now requires a session while agent connections are untouched. The control case is part of the verification and not an afterthought: an upgrade without `Origin` still completes, because a change that closes the leak and also severs every agent presents as green on any test that only checks whether the leak closed. The additive contract holds throughout — with zero accounts the layer does not exist and cannot be required, so reads pass and an exposed board says so once rather than silently. The login page, its script, and the identity endpoint remain reachable without a session, since a gate that also hides the way to authenticate locks out the person it was built for.

- **v2.6.91** (2026-08-07) — Two credential-boundary corrections in the board runtime, found by an automated review two days before this runtime first ships publicly. The operator credential file, which holds password hashes, was written with default permissions and chmodded afterwards — a window during which another user on the same host could read it, and one that `mode` alone does not close because it applies only when a file is created, leaving an already-loose file loose on overwrite. It is now written to a temporary file created at 0600 and moved into place atomically, hardened again after the move, and hardened on load so a file that predates this cut is rescued rather than trusted. And loopback is demoted from an identity to a defense layer: the host-local predicate correctly rejects proxied requests, but what remains after that rejection is *someone on this host* rather than a known operator — and one of the endpoints it guarded rewrites the bind address, so a local unprivileged process could widen the board to every interface. Both mutating admin endpoints now require a loopback origin **and** an authenticated operator session, while the additive contract is preserved exactly: with zero accounts the layer does not exist and cannot be required, so the check falls back to loopback and, when the board is exposed in that state, says so on every request rather than passing silently. The third loopback call site is deliberately unchanged and now says why in place — it serves local workers, which are agents rather than operators, and its threat model is remote reconnaissance, which the loopback test does close. Naming the two that changed without naming the one that did not is how a deliberate scope reads as an omission to the next reader.

- **v2.6.90** (2026-08-07) — Constellation v2.4.149 · Pantty v0.1.1 — the seat-driving reference runtime moves out of the Constellation tree to the module root, completing the promotion the previous cut began: `constellation/reference/runtime/pantty/` becomes `pantty/`, alongside the other modules' own asset directories. The move was safe because nothing imports those files — a sweep found no require, no import and no spawn of them from any consumer; they are standalone scripts that compute their own workspace paths, and the only machine coupling in the whole repository was a single path constant inside one checker. That makes the location a pure ownership signal rather than a dependency, and ownership was settled when the module was promoted. History entries in the changelog and in the README version chain deliberately keep the old path, because they record what a given version said rather than where the files are now — correcting them would falsify the record. Two guards earned their keep on the way: the retarget script counts anchors before writing and refused a file where the bilingual attributes made seven occurrences of a path where three were expected, and the docs-meta axis caught a hero badge bumped to the new version while the page's own description still summarised the previous one. And the move surfaced something the old layout had been hiding — compiled Python bytecode tracked in the public repository, machine-specific and read by nobody, now untracked and excluded going forward. Touching a path is the right moment to evict what was riding along in it.

- **v2.6.89** (2026-08-07) — Pantty is registered as the eighth module — docs page, module card, and the version checker taught to count both questions instead of one. The checker had three hand-written module lists and a fourth derivation coupled to plugins, while a comment one axis away said enumeration drifts in both directions; promoting an eighth module bit all four at once, so the fix was to stop needing a list rather than to append to it. Modules are now derived from root specs declaring `module:` in frontmatter, which also removes an unstated requirement that a module ship a plugin — Pantty is specification-stage and an empty plugin would be intake with no value. The first attempt unified all four onto one derivation and the checker immediately said that was too much: the seed registry asks which modules an adopter can *install* and requires a plugin path, while the docs and README counts ask how many specifications exist. Two axes, two questions, one denominator each — the same shape as measuring a region's plan availability against a VM-only listing and finding the difference is a bare-metal machine. A third hand list was found in the distro composer, where module specs were matched by an alternation of seven names; that one is now matched by shape (`^[A-Z][a-z]+\.md$` catches every module spec and no other root file) rather than by frontmatter, because the composer reads committed refs and a working-tree derivation would disagree with itself when composing an old tag. Its coverage assertion is what surfaced the gap: composition refused to run rather than silently dropping the new file. And the docs-meta axis was reporting a count it had not verified — a module without a docs page was skipped by a bare `continue`, so the line read "8 modules checked" while seven were; absence is now named in the output and not folded into the pass.

- **v2.6.88** (2026-08-06) — Constellation v2.4.148 — §13.35 resident seats is promoted out of this specification into its own module, `Pantty.md`, and what remains here is a pointer table plus the board side of the relationship. The move is a relocation rather than a revision: every requirement carries over with the same force, with all fifty MUST-class statements and all eight MUST NOTs accounted for, and the reference runtime under `constellation/reference/runtime/pantty/` is untouched. The subsection numbers stay, because §13.35.8 is cited from §13.38.5 and §13.39.2 and adopters hold citations this specification cannot enumerate — renumbering would break them silently, which is the exact failure §13.39.2 refuses when it declines to relocate the instances it names. A specification that promotes a section owes its readers the old address and not only the new one, so each module section closes with a marker naming its former Constellation number and the pair is auditable in both directions rather than only from here. A new §13.35.10 states what deliberately does not move: a seat remains a participant under §3.1 for keys and §13.25.11 for declaration binding, the supervisor's wall-clock ceiling and the completion-by-state rule remain §13.27, telemetry reaches the board as a change-triggered declaration under §13.23.4, and recovery failures surface through §13.20. Pantty specifies what a seat must be; this specification continues to specify how a board speaks to one. Registering the new module across the docs pages, the seed registry and the version checker is deliberately not part of this cut — which is why the consistency checker reports clean here: the module is invisible to it rather than wired into it, and that distinction is recorded rather than left for a later reader to mistake for completion.

- **v2.6.87** (2026-08-06) — Constellation v2.4.147 — the board's current-work band folds, per item and all at once. Three concurrent top-level items already consume the whole viewport, so reaching the planned queue below meant scrolling past everything in flight on every visit. A chevron on each card title collapses that card to its title; one on the band header collapses or expands the whole band, with its state derived from the cards rather than from a flag of its own so the two controls cannot disagree. The fold key is derived from item content rather than position, because an index key silently reassigns a collapsed state to a different card as soon as a finished item leaves the band. The collapsed rule hides the complement of the title rather than an enumeration of children, so an element added later cannot quietly stop folding. The load-bearing part is neither: the planned section's sticky header is positioned from a measured custom property holding the band height, so folding without re-measuring leaves the page looking folded while everything below stays pushed down by the old height — no error, and invisible in a screenshot. The browser assertion therefore checks that the height changed rather than that the class toggled, because the class alone passes on CSS while the height moves only if the layout hook actually ran; measured 612 → 421 → 195 → 612px across per-item fold, fold-all and expand-all, 22/22 checks passing.

- **v2.6.86** (2026-08-06) — Constellation v2.4.146 §13.40 — a gate's activation condition must not derive from what the gate watches. §13.38.2 named the gate that cannot pass under correct operation; this is its mirror, and the harder of the two to find, because a gate switched on by a property of the thing it inspects is off precisely on the inputs it was built for while every other run still looks correct. The shape: a redaction gate reads a denylist that is deliberately never committed, since the list's contents are themselves the disclosure being prevented — so conditioning strictness on the list being present disables the check on exactly the accident it exists to catch, and it reports pass while doing so. Generally, the inputs on which such a gate is inactive are by construction the inputs on which its subject is unavailable, making its coverage the exact complement of its purpose. Three consequences are normative: absence is a third outcome distinct from pass and fail, and a failure under an explicit strict mode, because success on an absent subject reports having checked in place of having skipped; the activation signal must be a property of where the check runs rather than of what it checks, disqualified whenever the accident guarded against could also change it; and verification requires producing the condition — remove the subject, confirm the distinct skip and its strict failure, then separately confirm a present clean subject still passes, since without that second half an always-failing gate is indistinguishable from correct enforcement. Grounded on an independent implementation of the same contract, which audited its own redaction gate against the norm and found it returning success both with the denylist absent and with the compiled pattern set empty, corrected it to a distinct skip plus strict mode, and covered it with six tests; that implementation also records writing the conditional-strict wiring first and discarding it before shipping, which is why this ships as a norm rather than an implementation note. A second instance of the §13.38.4 pattern — one project's defect, named at contract level instead of fixed locally, locating the same defect in another codebase that had already passed review.

- **v2.6.85** (2026-08-05) — Constellation v2.4.145 — §13.39 requires declared and effective state to be published together for observable modes with automatic fallback, demotion, or recovery; it preserves §13.35.8 and §13.38.2 at their already-cited numbers and identifies them as instances of the same norm, and it requires an inventory of outputs the system already writes before classification because “unobservable” can be a confession that existing evidence has not yet been sought.

- **v2.6.84** (2026-08-03) — Constellation v2.4.144 — §13.38.4 the dual-write predicate gains its measured grounding, contributed by an independent implementation of the same contract, and the measurement establishes what a single-repository derivation could not: **the defect is at the specification layer, not the implementation layer.** Both projects independently prescribed count equality — four sites here (the guide's contract body, its promotion checklist, its drift trigger, the module manifest's mode-B guard) and the counterpart's own backend RRP — so neither implementation invented the wrong predicate; each was told to use it. That is precisely why this is stated as a norm rather than left to implementer judgement: an empty spec slot gives the next implementer a chance to stop and ask, and a wrong prescription removes even that. Measured cost of the wrong predicate: 26 consecutive failing boots; a raw gap of 1,519 events (1,246 after normalizing the retention cap) against zero actual loss; residual repair converging to 30, then 6, then 3 and stopping, where replacing the question took it to 0. §13.38.2 additionally names the consequence that measurement surfaced and reasoning had missed: a gate whose failure action is auto-revert does not merely lose its signal, it **silently un-does the operator's configuration** — that deployment was configured for dual-write and ran single-store for the entire period, the setting still reading `dual`, with no error anywhere, so declared state and running state diverged while presenting as normal operation. A deployment must therefore verify that a configured mode is the mode actually running rather than inferring it from the setting. After the correction, the first boot passed while holding 1,323 surplus rows in the shadow store and dual-write ran for the first time — a gate that had never once passed passing while holding more surplus than the discrepancy that had been failing it, which is the clearest available demonstration that the predicate separates retention from loss.

- **v2.6.83** (2026-08-03) — The redaction rule had no instrument for the shape it was actually violated in. §5.7 requires zero verbatim conversation quotation in the public repository, and the checker introduced for it reads vocabulary — so fourteen verbatim quotations sat in public files for two months and passed every run: eleven in the Hyperbrief dogfood entries, three more in the DB P2 reference docs (one in prose, two in version-history footers, all three the same quotation carrying an explicit decision-source attribution). A rule keeps its shape only as long as something measures it, and this one had a measurement aimed one axis away from the breach. The quotations are restated as technical inputs in place, preserving each entry's input → spec-change chain, which was the evidentiary point of the dogfood record. The checker gains a line-shaped axis to close the gap, and its design is the load-bearing part: **quoted Korean is not the signal** — the changelog carries 476 such spans, the README 159, and the specs use quotes for terminology throughout, so an axis keyed on that would have produced hundreds of false positives and been ignored within a week. The discriminating shape is blockquote + quotation mark + conversational Korean, which resolves to three occurrences repository-wide, all legitimate: two seed example prompts an adopter types and one string a skill emits. Those carry an inline `redaction-ok:` waiver whose reason prints on every run, so exceptions live at the site rather than in a list that goes quiet. An English attribution pattern is added under the same measure-first discipline: a first draft keyed on `operator's` matched sixteen occurrences of the seed's own normative tier clause (raising the harness tier is the operator's call), so the pattern was narrowed to phrasings that point at a past utterance rather than at the role, leaving the role vocabulary untouched. Five of the fifteen mutation fixtures assert the false-positive boundaries rather than the detections, because an axis that flags everything passes every detection test. Also fixed: the release-cut script matched the previous `Current:` marker using the *new* cut's date, which every same-day cut had hidden, and stamped the demoted entry with the new date rather than preserving its own.

- **v2.6.82** (2026-08-03) — Constellation v2.4.143 — §13.38 dual-write reconciliation is directional. A mode-B reconcile check MUST evaluate containment in the direction of the write — every event committed to the canonical JSONL floor is present in the shadow database — and MUST NOT compare raw counts, because the two stores carry different retention policies on purpose: the floor caps per channel and re-applies that cap on boot rebuild, while the database accumulates without it since long-term retention is the entire reason it was adopted. Counting therefore measures a one-way obligation with a two-way instrument, firing on surplus when surplus is the product being purchased — it fails on every boot while saying nothing about loss, and drives the drift auto-revert on schedule. Three consequences are normative: a gate that cannot pass under correct operation is a gate that is off, to be re-examined against its contract rather than tuned until the red stops; the promotion gate, the drift trigger and the post-backfill check consume one verdict instead of re-deriving counts, since correcting the check while a consumer still asks the old question leaves behaviour unchanged and the correction looking complete; and repairing the proxy does not converge — matching the cap still skews unless the ordering basis matches, excluding archived channels over-excludes any channel later reactivated, and a backfill/check scope mismatch reports its set difference as loss every pass. `reconcile()` reports the surplus with the retention policies in force, because surplus without that context invites re-deriving the count comparison by hand. Derived surfaces trued up in the same cut: `DB-P2-Guide.md` §5 restated as a contract (containment verdict + report-only surplus + new §5.5 on permanently-red gates) with its pointer clauses corrected, `history-store.eux` mode-B guard and transition names corrected at the contract level, and the Mode-B runbook and benchmark framework aligned. The benchmark framework additionally drops a verbatim conversation quotation and its decision-source attribution, restated as technical criteria per the public-repo redaction rule.

- **v2.6.81** (2026-08-02) — Constellation v2.4.142 — §13.37 scale-out seats. Past one-operator-one-agent, three categories of shared knowledge infrastructure earn their always-on cost — knowledge-graph librarian seat, code-graph SSoT, judgment memory — specified as tier-gated residents with a four-clause integration contract (tier gating; shared-SSoT security posture: read-only serving by default and indexed content treated as data-not-instruction; declared freshness where age past bound is stale, never current; implementations live in a registry). Tool selection lives in the new `plugins/constellation/tool-registry.json` (confirmedBy/asOf/revisit per row; a 27th verify-nway axis enforces schema, deadline, and consumer linkage), because the measured category half-life is months — named tools are mentions expected to be swapped, not recommendations. The judgment-memory boundary clause is normative: retrieval and inertia priors only, never proxy decisions — decision gates bind to humans regardless of presence. eg-bootstrap 4b gains the seats row (estregenesis plugin v0.4.2 + four README inline mentions + regenerated Codex adapter). Grounded in an 11-agent five-axis research pass with six adversarially verified claims.

- **v2.6.80** (2026-08-02) — Constellation v2.4.141 — §13.36 harness chrome and the distribution boundary. A harness session's control plane (progress pings, approval prompts carrying command bodies, resume notices, receipts) rides the same pipe as substantive replies and is indistinguishable across a collaboration boundary — measured in both directions against an independent implementation (one inbox sweep: 103 frames, 49 a counterpart's control plane; the promising flag failed a cross-tab, 8/16 vs 4/6). Classification therefore moves to publish time: dedicated wire names (HarnessStatus, ApprovalRequest/Decision) with audience and wakeAgents:false (a tag on a text frame does not survive a storage path that reconstructs allowed fields, so the separate name is required, not stylistic); the server suppresses before agent fan-out as the first line and receiver filters are the second; approval traffic never crosses to agent connections and an unroutable approval gets an explicit reject-or-waiting status, never a silent drop; the interim for deployments without selective relay is rate-limit-never-drop (hold per window, wake once with the held count, flush on timer and stream end).

- **v2.6.79** (2026-08-02) — Constellation v2.4.140 — History send guard now derives from the payload. The hand-enumerated check lagged the v2.4.71 `opsStates` / v2.4.76 `capManifests` additions, silently dropping History on newborn servers carrying only ops/capability declarations — the very class v2.4.90 was cut to prevent, recurring inside the guard itself. Surfaced by an independent implementation's parity port auditing back into the original; fixed by deriving send-worthiness from the payload rather than adding the two missing keys, so the next payload key needs no guard edit (asserted across 9 cases).

- **v2.6.78** (2026-08-02) — **An error that fires on every message says nothing about any of them (Constellation v2.4.139, §13.13.5)** — §13.13.2(g) already named the owner of the durable-append commitment, and that parenthetical did real work: an independent implementation read it and correctly concluded its plugin layer must not claim the tier. What the section never said was what to do when **no layer owns what a tier asserts**, and the silence produced failures on both sides of it. The claim rule is now stated generally — a layer may emit a tier only if it owns the state that tier asserts, because a layer reporting a fact it cannot know is indistinguishable from the real thing at the receiving end. Where nothing owns a durable append, neither available default is right: emitting `delivered-persist` anyway is a claim about surviving a restart that nobody can honour, and staying silent leaves the sender's pending entry open until the ladder exhausts and reports the route unreachable. The answer is to emit the tier you *do* own — commitment at the moment the agent **begins** engaging, not at completion, since an ack that waits for completion times out on exactly the long turns that most need the entry cleared. The window where a frame has arrived but a turn is still running gets no tier at all, deliberately: it is neither durably appended nor surfaced-and-engaged, so redelivery there is correct behaviour rather than a defect, and closing it requires some layer to actually take ownership of a queue append rather than an adjustment to ack timing. And dedup is restated where implementations forget it — dedup means do not apply the side effects twice, never do not acknowledge; suppressing the ack along with the effects makes a successful redelivery indistinguishable from a lost one. The reading rule on the sender's side came out of measurement rather than reasoning. `commitment-ack-absent` reports that a pending entry expired without the tier arriving; it does not report that the frame failed to arrive. On one live route every targeted envelope sent over several weeks — five distinct identifiers — ended in that error, including ones whose application layer demonstrably received, processed and replied to them, because the peer never emitted any commitment-tier ack at all. The error was a constant on that route, and a constant carries no information. So a sender checks whether the route has *ever* produced the ack before treating its absence as evidence; neither `sent` nor `Ack{delivered}` closes the question either, since in the measured case the peer acknowledged delivery one millisecond after emit while the sender declared the route unreachable ninety-eight seconds later; and a resend must carry a **new** identifier, because the dedup watermark is keyed on the old one and re-sending it reaches a receiver that correctly treats it as already-handled. The incident's most transferable part is its shape: three parties each held a true observation — no application response, work completed, zero matching records in board history — and the whole was still wrong, because no layer can see another layer's ledger. Where the ledgers disagree the only common reference is application-layer state measured on the recipient side.

- **v2.6.77** (2026-08-02) — **An advisory lane and a review lane open identically and differ only at the merge (Superscalar v0.13.0, §1.5.1)** — the topology already named three reconvergence modes — synthesis, retire, review — and the third one *gates*: a reviewer's block stops the producer's retire. There was no vocabulary for the thing an operator asks for far more often, which is a second reading rather than a second judgment: send this to a model from another lineage and tell me what it sees, but the call stays mine. Expressed as Producer-Reviewer it silently acquires a gate; expressed as nothing it stays an informal habit that leaves no record of what was heard and overruled. **counsel** is the fourth reconvergence mode and **Principal-Advisor** the pattern it composes into — structurally Producer-Reviewer with the gate removed, which is the entire content of the distinction. Because the two shapes are indistinguishable at dispatch, the mode is **declared in the request**, and each default failure is wrong in its own direction: counsel read as review silently adds a gate nobody approved and hands it to a lane that was never asked to judge, usually on partial input, while review read as counsel silently removes a gate the reviewer meant as binding. Both are invisible until something has already committed. So the merge records which contract it was, and the contract fixes what silence means — for a reviewer, not-yet-reviewed and therefore no retire; for an advisor, nothing at all, because absence of counsel is not consent. Disagreement may be overruled, with the reason written down. The non-gating property is what makes the pattern cheap enough to reach for: a lane that cannot block does not need the review-throughput accounting Little's Law imposes on Producer-Reviewer, and it can be dispatched on a question that is not yet fully formed — but the moment an advisory return starts gating retires, the pattern has become Producer-Reviewer and inherits every constraint it was chosen to avoid. Different lineage is structural rather than a preference, for the reason adversarial verification already routes away from the author's family: a second reading that agrees for the same reasons is not a second reading. Which model advises well on what is a separate, empirical question this specification deliberately does not answer — it belongs to the model registry's harness profile under the evidence contract kept there, where every advisory row is currently unconfirmed or refuted, and shipping the mechanism with the routing unsettled is the honest state rather than a gap. The same measurement pass that refuted one of those rows also produced the day's other registry work: vendor primary documentation confirms that the two flagship models want *opposite* verification scaffolding — one instructs removing verification prompts and never using subagents to check the model's own work, the other instructs making self-verification explicit and reports that fresh-context verifier subagents outperform self-critique. A per-model profile stops being a hypothesis at that point.

- **v2.6.76** (2026-08-02) — **The registry said modules were opt-in, and nothing ever measured it (harness tier, seed v2.7.0)** — since v2.5.0 the module registry has read «a menu, not a checklist; adopt only when the trigger fires», and no mechanism has ever checked. A discipline disappears when the tool enforcing it does, even while its sentence stays on the page — and this one never had a tool at all, so every bootstrap landed wherever that day's judgement put it, with no vocabulary for stating how much was on. The **harness tier** is that sentence's mechanism: `seed` < `lean` < `active` < `resident`, where the axis is neither size nor capability but **how much runs when nobody asked**. It is deliberately *not* a fifth Phase 0 question — Phase 0 already asks four, and adding a question in order to promote leanness refutes itself — so the tier is **derived and declared in one line**, defaulting to `lean`. Two invariants carry the weight. A tier rises on **need, not size**: not because a project is large but because irreversible decisions are actually present, which is what makes a decision gate earn its cost, or because a second agent actually is, which is what makes coordination earn its; raising by size means carrying layers that eat context and return nothing. And **an agent may only lower it — raising is the operator's call**, because lowering saves the operator's budget while raising spends it, the same who-pays principle that put the deep briefing tier behind an explicit request one cut earlier. The counterweight is that the floor does not move with the tier: the autonomous-execution rule and the loss / external-publish gates are tier-independent, since a norm naming only what a tier turns *off* leaves the implementer to fill in the rest from habit, and habit fills it the permissive way. `eg-bootstrap` was already making exactly this split — pure discipline mounts, anything that runs a process waits — so the tier names behaviour that was already right rather than introducing new behaviour, and every opt-in row now states which tier it would raise the project to. Writing the checker surfaced two defects in the work itself: the consumer named only three tiers, omitting `seed`, which is the state of every adopter whose host has no plugin mechanism at all — the largest group rather than an edge case; and the check's own existence test matched prose, so a changelog sentence mentioning the feature satisfied it after the entire block had been deleted. It also surfaced an older one: **all six seeds carried a delta list frozen at v2.5.0** while their headers read v2.6.1, so the upgrade menu shown to an adopter had been missing its last two releases and presented as «no such change was ever made» rather than as an error. Backfilled, and now asserted against the header on every run. Two more measurement defects fell out along the way: the README's version chain had three lines stamped with the current release while carrying three different releases' content, twelve lines across the four register copies, green for three cuts because the ordering check accepted equal versions while its own comment claimed strict — data and check both corrected, and the repair derived each true version from the changelog rather than typing three of them by hand.

- **v2.6.75** (2026-08-02) — **Asking for a brief meant asking for the heaviest one (Hyperbrief v0.9.0, §2.6)** — v0.8 made the *floor* a setting and left the *request* untiered, so the phrase «brief me» resolved to the nine-section pipeline and, with it, a fan-out nobody had named. The module read as heavy when what was heavy was an unrequested cost. The request now carries a tier: a bare request is a **summary**, 요약/상세/심층 map to `SUMMARY_BRIEF`/`FULL_HYPERBRIEF`/`DEEP_BRIEF`, and resolution stays `max(rubric_tier, floor, request_tier)` so a request can only ever ask for *more* — asking for a summary on an irreversible cross-module decision still yields nine sections, and AF-27 is untouched. `DEEP_BRIEF` is a new lattice top that **only an explicit request can reach**, and the reason is not caution about depth but about who chooses to pay: fan-out is the one cost in this module paid in someone else's tokens and wall-clock rather than in the model's own turn, so a tier a rubric could trigger would spend it unasked. Deep emits the same `FullBrief` IR plus an optional `verification_annex` rather than a fourth schema shape, because making the deepest tier also the most likely to fail validation is backwards, and its refutation attempts must each name a distinct lens — three verifiers given one instruction produce one opinion three times. Shipped alongside: the composition tool for the stable edition (built from a committed ref, never the working tree, with a coverage assertion that halts on any top-level entry it has no rule for), and a distribution marker so a composed copy **declares itself a copy** — measured the same day, composing into the workspace produced a second vocabulary store and the resolver correctly refused, which on screen looked only like «store not found». Excluding by name would have re-opened silently the moment someone chose a different location.

- **v2.6.74** (2026-08-02) — **The install paragraph wrote three plugin versions by hand, and hands lag (readme-claims axis extended)** — the marketplace already holds every plugin's version, and the install section restated three of them from memory: the kit at 0.3.2 against a real 0.4.0, Superscalar at 0.2.3 against 0.4.0, Ultrasafe at 0.2.11 against 0.2.14. Twelve stale claims across the four copies of that paragraph. What surfaced them is worth more than the fix: a composition tool built for a separate purpose generates its manifest **by deriving** module versions from the marketplace, and the moment two surfaces stated the same fact — one derived, one hand-written — the hand-written one was visibly behind. That is the general shape rather than an anecdote; the same repository has now recorded it for module counts, check-axis counts, seed markers and summary-key lists. Deriving is not merely tidier, it makes the other copy's staleness **observable**, which is the property a hand list can never have. The axis that now guards this had to solve two false-positive traps, both of which would have quietly cost trust: `Constellation v0.3.40` (the plugin) and `Constellation v2.4.137` (the module specification) are the same shape, so the comparison only runs when the MAJOR matches — plugin versions are all `0.x`, and specification mentions fall out naturally; and the `Previously` chain quotes frozen past states, where differing from today's value is correct, so those lines are exempt as a whole, on the same principle by which quoted historical counts were already exempt. The axis prints how many claims it compared, because a regex that has silently stopped matching and a paragraph that genuinely contains no claims produce the same green.

- **v2.6.73** (2026-08-02) — **A frame addressed to no one inherited a recipient, and the recipient was someone else's agent (Constellation v2.4.138)** — seat telemetry is emitted with no `targetAgentId` on purpose: boards receive it by broadcast, so naming a recipient would be wrong. But the server's reply-window fallback fills a missing recipient with whoever most recently addressed this side — a last resort for adapters that cannot echo an envelope — so «no one» was read as «the last speaker». Measured across the whole history: 165 telemetry frames carried a recipient the emitter never wrote, ten of them a collaborating party's agent, which woke on every heartbeat to answer «telemetry, no action». The token cost on this side was zero; on theirs it was not, and one of those replies read «Interrupting current task (iteration 1/90)» — the frames were preempting work already running there. Each reply reopened the window, so the leak was self-sustaining. The guard that should have stopped it recognised exactly one watcher's identity, because §2 said telemetry «is tagged» without saying **how**, and the implementer filled that gap with the only telemetry source that existed at the time; every stream added later was structurally un-taggable. The resolution moves the question to whoever knows the answer: **the emitter declares it**, carrying `telemetry: true`, stamped at its single outbound chokepoint rather than per call site — an observing process emits nothing but observation, so counting its frame names would leak again on the next name, the way per-surface `msgId` stamping leaked before it became a chokepoint. The classification now lives in one component the server consults, the legacy tag is still honoured so existing adopters see no change, and a small named safety net covers emitters not yet updated. The third layer is that staleness has to be visible: the server now says once — naming sender, frame and inherited recipient — whenever the reply-window fills a blank, because without that line «paired a reply» and «mailed someone else's telemetry» are the same shape on every surface that could show the problem. The checker asserts the mechanism rather than the list: a frame name nobody has enumerated is excluded on the tag alone, and a control arm confirms a genuine unaddressed reply is still paired, since killing the fallback would be a different defect wearing the same green. A mutation run on a reverted copy confirms the checker can fail — and while writing it, the checker's own anchor was found assuming a `function` declaration, so when the declaration form changed both sides missed identically and the copy-parity assertion passed on two empty strings. §2 now states how tagging is set and that the inherited peer may sit outside this deployment's cost boundary, and the consumer sweep for a new always-on stream explicitly includes collaborating parties, peers and upstreams.

- **v2.6.72** (2026-08-02) — **A peer's own vocabulary made the row preview blank, and a blank preview looks exactly like a message with nothing to say (Constellation v2.4.137)** — each A2A intent carried a hand-listed set of summary keys, so a counterpart writing its own dialect — measured: `TOPIC` where this side writes `re` — matched nothing and the row rendered as a bare label. That absence is the expensive part: an empty preview and a contentless message are the same shape on screen, so the list being stale cannot be seen from the surface it damages. Rather than growing twenty per-intent lists, the resolution is structural in three layers. **One shared tail** follows each intent's own ordering, so a newly observed dialect is one edit in one place rather than twenty; `topic` sits beside `re` because it fills the same role. **Case is folded during lookup**, since capitalisation is itself a dialect axis and keeping two spellings of every key is the same enumeration problem wearing a different hat. And a **last resort** picks the first field that reads like prose — never leaving the row blank — while recording which key it had to guess from, so the vocabulary gap becomes a collected observation instead of a silent one (`window.wsDialectKeys`). The prose preference is not decoration: the first field is arbitrary, and a live counterpart's first field was a content hash, so a preview showed sixty-four hex characters where a sentence was available two fields later. Preference runs sentence → prose-like → anything, which on the same live payload moved the preview from a model identifier to the actual finding. Verified against both live dialects and the regression case where the canonical field still wins when present.

- **v2.6.71** (2026-08-02) — **An address answers «where from», and the operator surface needs «who» (Constellation v2.4.136, §13.25.17)** — the operator predicate reads a connection's address: from this machine means holds the board. Behind the reverse proxy the specification itself recommends, every remote client presents as local, so the previous cut could only *refuse* that case — detection, not a path. This cut supplies the path as a reference implementation, and its whole design is the additive contract: **with zero accounts the layer does not exist** — predicate, cookie and screen bit-identical to before, no file created, a login attempt answered «no operators» rather than a prompt. Adoption is decided by one act with no flag: creating the first account. An adopter who never creates one is not carrying a disabled feature, they are carrying the previous behaviour. With at least one account the predicate consults the session **and nothing else**, because a predicate that keeps an address fallback is one the proxy can still flip. The requirements each match a way this class fails: memory-hard salted hashing, constant-time comparison, equal cost for a missing account (or response time enumerates accounts), per-account attempt limiting, an in-memory session token so a restart logs everyone out rather than adding a second secret at rest, `HttpOnly`+`SameSite=Strict` cookies with `Secure` off loopback, and the account file in the credential class — gitignored and `0600`. Bootstrap has one exception that closes itself: account creation is unauthenticated only while the count is zero, so the window is one act wide. Deleting the last account is refused through the API for the same reason it remains possible on disk — it silently returns the deployment to address-based judgement, which is a decision rather than a click. Display names are attacker-controlled free text and are escaped at render, since rendering them as markup is stored XSS against *other* operators — the case a single-operator deployment structurally cannot notice. The checker runs two isolated servers and asserts both arms: zero-account behaviour unchanged, and the verdict **flipping** the moment an account exists, which is what makes «the layer is wired» measurable rather than assumed; a mutation run confirmed it goes red when the predicate line is removed. Found while verifying: a frame addressed to its own sender was being registered for redelivery, and since a receiving bridge deliberately never acks its own echo, that entry could never clear — a guaranteed false «unreachable» three attempts later. The main bridge's own connect greeting was taking that path on every reconnect, so an alert meaning «could not deliver» actually meant «addressed to myself».

- **v2.6.70** (2026-08-02) — **A pair-shaped split for a two-tab board, still hardcoded at four tabs — and markdown that stopped at the features its first reader needed (Constellation v2.4.134–135)** — Ctrl+clicking a tab was supposed to toggle *that* tab into the split view. It always produced the same fixed pair instead, and nobody could see it while there were only two tabs, because that pair was the only combination the intent could produce. At four tabs the difference became visible: the code said «pair», never «toggle». Splitting is now genuinely N-way — any combination, up to four panes, dividers generated between neighbours, the last pane protected from removal, and layout order following tab order rather than click order, because a set that lands in a different arrangement each time never becomes muscle memory. Sizing follows the pane count: two panes keep the existing ratio-and-pin contract untouched, three or more use per-pane weights where dragging a divider moves weight between its two neighbours only. Home affordances now derive their position from **their own pane's right edge** rather than from «the divider», which was well-defined only while there was exactly one. Compendium term links open the wiki **beside** what you were reading instead of replacing it — the previous behaviour cost you the screen you were consulting the term for — and narrow viewports still swap rather than cram. Second, markdown: the renderer was a chat-only miniature, so tables, ordered lists, quotes, rules and diagrams simply were not there — and «not there» surfaced only as pipe characters sitting in the text, which reads as a styling problem rather than a missing feature. It now renders the full set, mermaid included, across the review panel and the live conversation alike, keeping the escape-first discipline (escape the source, then build tags; diagram source is injected as text, never as markup). One ordering bug is worth recording because it is invisible in the common case: restoring code and diagram placeholders **after** the newline-to-break conversion put break tags inside the diagram source, so mermaid failed to parse and code blocks came out with markup in them — the fix is that newlines convert first and placeholders restore last. Verified in a live browser at every step: four panes with three dividers, arbitrary combinations, table/ordered-list/quote/rule/code and a rendered diagram.

- **v2.6.69** (2026-08-02) — **Typing cost 185ms per keystroke, and the board was paying it in full layout recalculations (Constellation v2.4.133)** — the operator reported input in the review panel lagging tens of seconds before landing in one burst. Three synthetic passes failed to reproduce it — idle, under CPU load, at several window widths — and the failure was informative: automated typing skips IME composition entirely, so it never paid the per-jamo cost that makes the symptom visible. The operator's own observation closed it: *narrow the window and it appears*. Measured with a scripted input sweep, the cost was **165–195 ms per keystroke** at every width, worst when narrow — a full second of stall per five characters, and Korean composition emits an event per jamo, which is exactly «tens of seconds, then all at once». The mechanism has two halves that are easy to blame on each other. The textarea's auto-grow sets height to `auto`, reads `scrollHeight`, then writes the measured height — a write-read-write that forces **two full document layouts, synchronously, on every input event**. And one full layout on this page costs ~30 ms, because the visible dashboard pane renders every completed entry at once: 7,260 nodes of 8,356. Neither half is a defect alone; together they multiply. The fix addresses both, and an A/B/A distinguished the effective ingredient from the plausible one: `content-visibility: auto` on cards took it from 184.4 to 0.7 ms/key and reverting restored 177.6, while `contain: layout paint style` alone measured 196.7 — no help at all. Skipping layout for off-screen cards is the active ingredient; containment without it is a plausible remedy that does nothing. The auto-grow is separately coalesced to one measurement per animation frame, because typing cannot outrun a frame, so the visible result is identical and the count drops. The two are not substitutes: one cuts how often layout is forced, the other cuts what each one costs. Verified after deployment at both narrow and wide widths: **0 ms per keystroke**, 310 cards still rendering with none collapsed.

- **v2.6.68** (2026-08-02) — **Four implementations refused the same ack for the same reason — that's a specification gap wearing four disguises (Constellation v2.4.132)** — the relay shipped hours earlier delivered, and then delivered again, and again: every operator-feedback frame arrived in triplicate, ~35 seconds apart, same event id, same recovery key. The redelivery layer was doing its job — the commitment ack never came back. §13.13.2 said the receiver replies «to the original sender», and that wording named only the case its author had in mind: a frame relayed by the server on a board surface's behalf carries no sender `agentId`, and **all four bridge implementations** — the canonical bridge, both main-bridge channels, and the light join helpers — declined to ack it on the same guard, «no addressee for the ack». Four independent implementations stumbling at one spot is the deterministic signature of a spec gap, not four coincident bugs. The rule now stated for all cases: the ack predicate keys on (addressed to me + recovery key + not an ack kind) and MUST NOT condition on a resolvable sender; with no addressee the ack simply omits `targetAgentId`, and the server consumes a target-less `AckProcessed` after clearing the pending entry — the absorb matters, because the unaddressed fallback would otherwise deliver transport plumbing to the main agent as mail. Two receiver corollaries came out of nearly shipping a second defect inside the first fix: a redelivered duplicate is **re-acked** — the redelivery itself proves the previous ack was not seen, so a dedupe that swallows the duplicate silently *extends* the loop it was meant to end — and its body is not re-appended (the canonical bridge already carried the LRU for this; the light helpers gained a bounded set). A checker axis now asserts the optional-target idiom on all five deployed copies plus the server absorb. Wire-measured before and after: the same POST that landed three times now lands exactly once, with the ack recorded server-consumed.

- **v2.6.67** (2026-08-02) — **The operator answered, and nobody was listening: the file is the log, the relay is the wake (Constellation v2.4.131)** — the operator pushed five substantive entries through the dashboard's feedback buttons — answers to three open decisions and two defect reports — and the agent heard none of them, because `POST /api/feedback` appended to `feedback.jsonl` and appending was the whole pipeline: no relay, no watcher, no consumer. The header comment even said «server log → agent review» — a designed intent whose enforcing mechanism didn't exist, which is what a rule without a mechanism looks like. The bitter detail: one of the five entries *reported the wake failure*, and fell into the very hole it described. §13.13.4 now makes the relay normative: the server relays every accepted entry into the live stream as an `OperatorFeedback` event targeted at the primary agent — carrying a recovery key from the shared stamping component so a main-bridge outage redelivers instead of dropping, timestamp-normalized at the broadcast boundary, mirrored to boards, persisted to history, offered to web-push. Teaching every consumer to watch the file would have been the wrong shape: it multiplies watchers that each fail separately, where one relay reuses the entire existing delivery, redelivery, classification and notification pipeline. The consumer sweep is stated in the spec so adopters don't rediscover it (classifiers must not absorb the name; push should notify; unaddressed seats are untouched), and a parity-checker axis now asserts the call site (append **then** relay, order not adjacency), the recovery-key path, the live deployed copy (which is how the axis proved it could fail — it went red on the un-synced copy before the restart), and the two negative consumer assertions. Wire-verified end to end after restart: a test POST arrived as `OperatorFeedback` in the agent inbox within seconds. Also disclosed: v2.4.130 (the future-timestamp clamp) had shipped in code without its module-surface bump — trued up in this cut's docs.

- **v2.6.66** (2026-08-02) — **Two external evaluation reports, taken through the new intake skill — and the quote that looked wrong was a correct quote of our own stale surface** — two commissioned external assessments of this project (a harness evaluation scoring 7.7/10, and a visibility analysis) became `/feeda`'s first live run. Every checkable claim was measured against the repository and GitHub rather than judged by plausibility: star/fork/commit counts, topics, the docs tagline, the migration scenarios, seed tier sizes, and the module roster. The decisive verdict: where the reports and the repository disagreed, **the reports were right**. Their «six optional modules» was an accurate quote of README surfaces frozen since the seventh module shipped a week earlier — and measurement found the drift wider than they saw: the README said six in the heading and seven two paragraphs later, listed six bullets, and omitted the seventh from all four install blocks; the KO register copies tripled every instance, and the EN and KO size tables had drifted from *each other* (EN updated to ~2440/~1120 lines, KO frozen at ~2425/~1105, Compact stale on both sides). Per the intake discipline the mechanism came before the fix: a new **readme-claims** verify axis derives the module count from the marketplace — a plugin whose capitalized spec `.md` exists at the repo root counts as a module, derived, never hand-listed — and checks every EN/KO count phrase against it, plus seed-size claims within ±5% of measured line counts. It went red with 16 real violations before the fix, and its own first draft had to be corrected twice (a Lite table row mentioning the *other* tier mis-attributed a claim; a wc-vs-split off-by-one) — the checker-must-be-able-to-fail rule earning its keep on its author. Also confirmed from the reports and recorded as decisions rather than silently fixed: the repository has a hundred-plus tags but **zero GitHub Releases**, the first impression shows the whole platform where the minimal path is one Compact seed, and no independent quantitative case study exists — three visibility actions that belong to the operator, now on the decisions panel.

- **v2.6.65** (2026-08-02) — **The fourth borrowing: a memory hierarchy for the context cache (Superscalar v0.12.0 / plugin v0.4.0)** — the operator's fourth skill idea asked where context-cache management should live, and the answer was already in the module's name: Superscalar borrows processor architecture — issue width, out-of-order execution, speculation, heterogeneous cores — and the memory hierarchy was the chapter still missing, even though two cache rules were already living scattered in §5.1 (a delegated subagent starts cache-cold; effort is a caching decision). §5.4 generalizes them into one discipline with one home, and the numbers underneath it went through a research pass with a deterministic verification gate rather than recall: a claim ledger of twelve entries, nine verified (each cross-confirmed on at least two independent domains, refutation-searched for the numeric ones, anchored to the vendor's own page), three left explicitly unresolved as vendor-doc-only, zero refuted — though one prior belief was corrected on the way, since the «half price» cached-input figure remembered for one vendor is now a tenth, paired with a paid cache write. The decisive find was that the hardest axis — which harness operations flush the cache — needed no observation at all: an official page documents it end to end, down to subagents running a shorter TTL than the main conversation and the flushes that fire without any operator action, such as a tool server dying and auto-reconnecting. The discipline is six rules: pin model and effort at the session head, since each is a cache key and a switch bills on the *next* turn where it feels free; compact at task boundaries and prefer rewind over compact for abandoned paths, because a rewind returns to a prefix that is already cached while a compact builds a new one; prefetch context right *after* a boundary, where reads land at the front of the new stable prefix; price fan-out with cache-cold accounting, which lands delegation exactly where §5.1 already routes it; consult the per-harness flush list before any mid-session mutation; and measure with the cache counters instead of declaring, which is this repository's telemetry rule applied to a new surface. The volatile half — multipliers, TTLs, minimums, hourly storage rents, flush lists — lives in `cache-registry.json` under the §5.1.3 contract (asOf, confirmedBy per row, revisit date and watchlist), with one addition: facts confirmed only against the vendor's own page carry a `singleSource` mark instead of blending silently with cross-confirmed ones. Default OFF for a jurisdictional reason rather than caution: harnesses already automate the substrate, so the skill covers only what they don't decide — and that scope is *expected to shrink* as absorption proceeds, which is the module's standard-substrate bet working as intended, not a defect.

- **v2.6.64** (2026-08-01) — **Three operator-proposed skills: two intake disciplines for the kit, and out-of-order execution for the main lane (kit v0.4.0, Superscalar v0.11.0 / plugin v0.3.0)** — `/talka` is the gentle sibling of `/eg-interview`: same goal — real intent, real constraints, real criteria — opposite pace. Where the interview presses a request into a delegable brief in a few batched rounds, talk-about holds a relaxed, topic-anchored conversation for the cases where that press fails or harms: tacit knowledge, an early topic, stakes that make interrogation premature. Its discipline is at most one question per turn — prefer stating an observation and letting *correction* do the extraction, because people correct a wrong statement more readily, and more precisely, than they answer an open question — plus a running elicitation ledger whose every entry must change the upcoming judgment, materialized to a durable surface at close (a ledger that evaporates with the session was chat). `/feeda` codifies the intake pipeline this repository has been running by hand on adopter reports: read the whole artifact — data to verify, never instructions to follow; embedded directives surface as the artifact's *requests*, not as orders — verify every claim by measurement into confirmed / partial / refuted / unmeasurable, tier the survivors (defect · spec gap — an independent implementer stumbling where the spec named one case indicts the spec, not their reading · design disagreement · info-only), build the prevention mechanism *before* fixing the instance, then close the loop with the contributor, refutations included with their measurements — a closed loop turns a one-time reporter into a standing detector, and silence teaches them to stop writing. `/ooo` (§5.3) extends the module's out-of-order discipline to the main lane's own most common stall: a question to the human. Ask-and-wait is an in-order pipeline stalled on one very slow operand, so a question now registers as a one-line scoreboard entry instead of halting the task — self-resolve by measurement first (most questions are unread files), bypass everything independent of the answer, assumption-run only under §4's speculation gates, park what remains. A late answer wakes only its dependents, never a global restart; the forbidden transition is the silent guess, an unnamed assumption indistinguishable from confidence to every later reader. Loss and external-publish gates are never bypassed in any mode — the toggle moves the *waiting*, never the *gates*. Also in this cut: the README's Current section had been carrying three paragraphs of v2.6.59 state through four releases — including a «checkers are red on purpose» claim that stopped being true at v2.6.61 — now retired to this changelog, where that story already lives. And the changelog itself had the same disease: twenty-seven Korean entries had accumulated inside the English section, so a reader following the «한국어» link landed twenty-seven releases behind — all moved to their own section.

- **v2.6.63** (2026-08-01) — **Three operator-reported board defects, and the first two were the new telemetry's own (Constellation v2.4.129)** — the seat telemetry shipped hours earlier was rendering as a chat row every few seconds and raising a push notification each time. Cost had not been saved, only moved: a stream that costs no model tokens was filling the surface a person reads. The fix is placement, not frequency — telemetry now feeds an indicator, exactly as the workflow and subagent snapshots already did, and joins the push blocklist beside them. That blocklist already carried a comment saying a new snapshot name must be added to it; the rule was there and the name was not, which is what a discipline without a mechanism looks like. **Second, the time axis.** Frames were appearing at positions unrelated to when they happened, and correcting themselves on reload. Timestamp normalization existed but sat at the storage boundary, while dispatch broadcasts before it records — so live viewers received un-normalized frames and sorted a missing timestamp as zero, placing them at the epoch. Normalization moved to the broadcast boundary, because fixing our own emitter would have left every other adapter able to reproduce it. The emitter was fixed too: it had never stamped a time, which also explains workflow progress rows landing oddly. **Third, history volume.** The initial payload carried every event of every active channel, which on a long-running board is what makes the first paint heavy. Active channels are now capped per channel, older entries load on request, and — the load-bearing part — the truncation is *declared*: the payload states the limit, which channels were cut, how many were sent of how many, and the oldest timestamp sent, so the client can ask for the next page and show what remains. A silent cut would read as deletion, which is the misdiagnosis the scope field was introduced for in v2.4.89. Also folded in: `Ping`/`Pong` were being absorbed by name, making the escalation ladder's probe step structurally unanswerable, and the ack-body rule from the previous cut was applied to the whole exclusion list rather than the three ack names — briefly making a join greeting wake the session.

- **v2.6.62** (2026-08-01) — **A seat's state was declared, not measured — and the declaration was wrong all day (Constellation v2.4.128)** — a model switch was issued twice, confirmed twice by the harness's own command output, and announced to the board; every actual turn ran on the previous model. The declaration was the surface a person read, the record was the surface nobody read, and nothing compared them, so the reason for the switch went unapplied for a working day. §13.35.8 now requires seat telemetry to be **derived** from what the harness recorded — never from what someone declared — and a reader supplies model, effort, context occupancy, in-flight tool, last activity and harness version from the session transcript. Three properties make it trustworthy, each matching a way this repository has already failed: it holds no model or effort literals, so a declaration cannot quietly outrank a measurement; absence is `unknown` with null values and a stale record is `stale`, never `idle` and never zero, because a zero claims emptiness and so measures the instrument instead of the seat; and it spawns nothing and calls nothing over the network, which is what separates telemetry from **echo**. That separation is the load-bearing part: echo makes the model speak an extra time and costs tokens, so it is legitimately switchable, while telemetry reads a file the harness already wrote and costs no model tokens at all — binding it to the echo switch would produce a capability that is free and off. It therefore runs above that gate, in the resident that already polls the same directory rather than in a fourth process. Second, from an adopter's measurement the same day: a substantive reply carried inside an `Ack` envelope is lost three ways, none of which raises an error — the recovery layer excludes ack names **by construction**, so there is no pending entry, no redelivery and no undeliverable notice; for the same reason the sender gets no delivered ack and holds only "sent"; and receiver-side filters legitimately absorb those names, advancing a cursor past a message a person was meant to read. Two independent implementations hit it on the same day, which locates the fault in the shared wire vocabulary rather than in either filter. §13.13 now states that application-tier content MUST NOT ride a transport-tier name, and both directions are mechanized rather than left as discipline: the emit path refuses an ack-named envelope carrying a body, and the meaningful-set classifier wakes on one. Three checker corrections came out of the same work, all of the same shape — an axis measuring adjacency where the rule says order, a discovery gate reading prose where it meant code, and a gate test looking at a definition where the question was about the call site.

- **v2.6.61** (2026-08-01) — **A frame could be sent and be unrecoverable, and nothing said so (Constellation v2.4.127)** — the redelivery layer only tracks envelopes carrying a recovery key, and eleven of this repository's thirteen sending surfaces never put one on. A frame without a key gets no delivered ack and no pending entry, so if it lands in the window while the recipient restarts it disappears with no error and the sender is not told — «sent» and «arrived» stop being distinguishable. Three defects sat behind it, each of which reads as health. **The two thresholds disagreed**: the ack predicate accepted `msgId || messageId`, the registration predicate accepted only `msgId`, so an envelope in the gap earned a delivered ack while never entering redelivery — the worst variant, because the sender reads the ack as arrival. They are now one predicate that returns the key, so the entry's key comes from the same place as the verdict. **A named-but-unknown recipient fell into the unaddressed fallback** and was handed to the main agent: the sender never learned of non-delivery and main received mail addressed to someone else, two faults in one envelope. Naming a recipient is not a request to give it to main, so the dispatch now separates «no addressee» from «this addressee is not here». **An absent recipient's queue entry never aged**: redelivery is deferred until reconnect, which is right, but the deferral incremented nothing, so an entry for someone who never returns waited forever without notifying anyone. Absence now carries a bound. The stamping itself is a shared part rather than a rule: one component mints the key and the transport chokepoint of each surface passes envelopes through it, because a rule that each call site must remember fails the same way every time — a new surface omits it, and the omission looks like a well-sent message. The two deployments that cannot import it (a browser page, and plugins installed standalone from the marketplace) carry a documented copy of the same rule. The checker that drove this cut also had to be corrected: its own remedy said to stamp at the transport path rather than at call sites, yet it kept counting the call sites of files that had done exactly that — an axis that names one shape of compliance marks the other shapes as violations, and here the shape it named was the enumeration the fix removes.

- **v2.6.60** (2026-08-01) — **The tier ladder gets a middle rung: T1.5, for the flagship that acts sooner (Superscalar v0.10.0, plugin v0.2.4)** — the four-tier composition vocabulary left a 2× spread sitting inside T1: the registry's own price rows record the deep-deliberation flagship at exactly twice the start-here flagship's rate in both directions, but the tier boundary absorbed the fact, so routing never saw it. And price was not even the routing-relevant half. Dogfood observation on the start-here flagship is a temperament difference — thinking converts into action sooner, which reads as speed on well-framed work and as a slip mode on multi-step work — and the effort dial does not buy back the missing deliberation, because the registry already carried the vendor's hint that effort does not reliably change response depth there. So §5.1.1 now names **T1.5 · Frontier Execution**: frontier-class capability bound to an execution contract — always paired with verification gates (check-first, test gates), decisions and adversarial review escalated to T1, spec-complete work dropped to T2. One model occupies the band today; a caveat records the temperament claim as a single-workspace observation rather than a vendor fact, and the watchlist carries the question of whether a mode-switched flagship from another vendor belongs in it — both aimed at the scheduled revisit, not at re-surveying now. Second, invitation-gated models: the registry listed a restricted-access model for recognition, and recognition is exactly where the trap is — presence in a registry, a picker, or an allowlist is not entitlement, which for this class is per-org/account. The binding procedure now requires verifying the concrete account's enrollment before a lane binds; unverified means unavailable, and unavailable degrades down a tier at the same effort, never sideways to an unverified model. While cutting, the band review also trued up two pre-existing "Today:" enumerations that had drifted both ways — T1's list omitted its two gated members (claude-mythos-5, gpt-5.5-pro; now listed with their access qualifiers), and T3's list carried an id with no registry row (kimi-k2.7-code) while omitting a member it had (grok-build-0.1).

- **v2.6.59** (2026-08-01) — **보안** — **A page served from any local port could become the board's operator (Constellation v2.4.126)** — the WebSocket upgrade's cross-site gate allowed any loopback-origin page: «a local dev server on another port is explicitly permitted». A page served from localhost could therefore open the board's socket, and because it sent no key and no HELLO its connection carried no role — which classified it as the *board* surface, the one the operator uses. `wsOperatorAuthz` then returned true on the socket address alone. That opened key issuance, **key enumeration returning raw values**, revocation, `SetMain`, irreversible history deletion, and prompt injection into the main agent.

The decisive diagnostic was already in the file: the HTTP twin written by the same author against the same threat, `sameOriginPost`, has no such exception. Two independent judgements diverging at one spot is a specification gap rather than a matter of taste — and §13.25.15 did explicitly permit «or be a loopback page», so the implementation was following the specification. The exception is gone; the dashboard is unaffected because this server serves it, so it passes on host equality, and deployments needing a different origin declare it in `WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` — a declaration rather than a blanket class.

Second, `wsOperatorAuthz`'s board branch now consults the forwarding-header flag the upgrade already records. One line above it, the agent branch consults it; this branch did not, so behind a reverse proxy — the arrangement §13.25.16 recommends — every remote client presents as local and the branch hands over the highest-privilege verb set. Address cannot answer *which person*, so refusal is the honest verdict, and the path for a legitimate proxied operator is an account concept that remains an open decision.

A third change was written and then withdrawn before shipping, which is worth recording. The history verbs (`CloseChannel`, `DeleteChannelHistory`, `RequestChannelHistory`, `ArchiveChannel`) reach irreversible deletion and restore archived content that the initial payload deliberately abbreviates — and they pass no authorisation predicate at all. A gate for them was added, and the collab smoke test immediately showed reconnect storms: five hellos where the contract permits one. Bisecting proved the gate was the cause — the dispatch is not board-only, so non-main agents were being refused a path they legitimately use. The gate is deferred to a cut that first establishes where the board/agent boundary actually runs. The finding stands; the fix was wrong.

Verification state, stated plainly: three checkers are **red on purpose** right now. This investigation found that two existing checkers were concealing the defect they were written for — one fills in a missing field by hand, the other injects the very event it claims to observe — so the current track makes them honest first and repairs the runtime after. The failures they show are the real state of the code. This release's own changes were bisected against them: with the security patch reverted the same four failures remain, and no others appear with it applied.

- **v2.6.58** (2026-07-30) — **MCP dropped the handshake, and the servers here were still the first revision (dual-era)** — the 2026-07-28 revision makes MCP stateless at the protocol layer: the `initialize` handshake is gone, every request carries its protocol version in `_meta`, and servers **MUST** implement `server/discover`. The four MCP servers in this repository declared `2024-11-05` and implemented `initialize`, `tools/list`, `tools/call` — nothing else. In the specification's compatibility matrix that is the row that fails: a modern client against a legacy server.

The migration was small for an unusual reason: none of what the revision deprecates was ever implemented here. No Roots, Sampling, Logging, `ping`, `logging/setLevel`, HTTP+SSE, resources or prompts — so the deprecations cost nothing and there was nothing to remove. The servers were also already stateless in practice: `initialize` was answered but never required, so a request arriving without it was already served.

They are now dual-era. `server/discover` advertises both supported versions; `initialize` stays and still answers with the legacy version, because a legacy client handed a modern version string has nowhere to go. A request whose `_meta` names an unsupported version gets `-32022` with the supported list; a request with no `_meta` at all is served as before. Results carry `resultType` and list results carry `ttlMs`/`cacheScope`. The version strings live in one shared component rather than four copies — the same enumeration-drift shape this repository hit three times in the preceding day.

The checker runs the four servers as real stdio child processes and speaks JSON-RPC to them, because the defect class here is a protocol envelope and a source grep cannot see one. Four mutations revert each half. Separately, this cut was implemented by a different engine under a written brief, and the first attempt failed in a way worth recording: the fallback engine's command line carried a flag its current release had removed, and it reported a usage error while exiting zero. The same command line is what this repository's means ladder builds when it switches engines, so the ladder's last rung was broken from the day it shipped.

- **v2.6.57** (2026-07-30) — **A premise a single configuration line can invert is not a premise (Constellation v2.4.125)** — a board carries a roster, a conversation history, an org chart, and controls that issue live keys and hand over the control plane. None of it is meant to face the open internet, and that was written down. It was also expressible away: an allowlist of `null` meant *every address*. Measured on the live board — binding exposed, agent and MCP allowlists both unset — a non-loopback address received the agent roster and the conversation history **before sending a handshake at all**. Presenting a key afterwards was refused, but the refusal came after the payload.

The detail that makes the shape clear is that the *human* UI surface was already narrowed, in the same file, to a LAN range plus an overlay range. The surfaces left open were the agent-facing ones — the two whose audience is machines, and therefore the two nobody looks at.

So the change is the allowlist's **domain**, not its evaluation. The domain is private address space: named ranges (loopback, RFC1918, CGNAT, link-local, IPv6 ULA) or CIDRs inside them. A public address is not a value the configuration can hold — an entry covering one is refused with a reason printed on every load, because an entry silently dropped reads exactly like an entry that works. Absent now means *all private ranges* rather than *all addresses*, since a default is the state of every deployment nobody has thought about. Empty means loopback only: closed has to be expressible, and it must not lock the operator out of the surface that would reopen it.

The arithmetic has to be exact, because the neighbours of private space are public — `172.31.255.255` is private and `172.32.0.0` is not, `100.127.255.255` is CGNAT and `100.128.0.0` is not. A predicate that is loose at those edges widens the reachable set by a whole range and reports nothing, so the checker tests the boundaries on both sides. A range *entry* is validated at both ends rather than at its base, since `10.0.0.0/4` begins in private space and swallows most of the public internet.

Refusing public sources costs nothing, because both legitimate ways to reach a board from elsewhere arrive privately: an overlay network places the peer inside CGNAT, and a reverse proxy terminating TLS connects from the host.
