All of them were addressed to this agent by name — **being addressed is itself the evidence**, and requiring the name to also be pre-registered discards information the envelope already carries. The decision is now a **union**: the allowlist stays as a floor, and an envelope addressed to this agent that is not transport or telemetry is meaningful regardless of its name. Three first-attempt errors are recorded because the corrected rule is only defensible against them. **(1) Union, not replacement** — replaying the same window with the inversion *replacing* the allowlist gave **−16%**, losing `Report` ×148, `UserPrompt` ×57 and `RelayUnreachable` ×22; the last is the name added two cuts ago *specifically* so delivery-failure notices would stop being lost, so a replacement would have re-opened the hole the floor was built for. **(2) No "agent-authored" predicate** — the wire's `source` is not limited to `agent`: user utterances arrive as `source:"board"` and delivery failures as `source:"server"`, and those two are the *most* actionable authors, so a rule gated on agent-authorship excludes exactly the wrong things. The test is not who wrote it but whether it was addressed here. **(3) No numeric threshold** — the brief that proposed this carried a "more than 10 per turn" cap chosen without measuring; the measured cost of the union is **+10 envelopes over 60.2 days (0.17/day, +2%)** of which 9 are substantive, so the cap would have written an unmeasured number into the contract. Identity is required for the second branch and its absence is **announced**: without a declared `SELF_AGENT_ID`/`CONSTELLATION_AGENT_ID` the branch is inactive and the probe says so on stderr rather than degrading silently to the floor. And the cut found a second defect while making the change: this classification lives in three copies, prior cuts asserted their **name sets** matched — which they did — while the **logic** had diverged. Two copies were missing the v2.5.44 self-emission gate (`ev === "sent"`), so an agent's own outbox pushes surfaced to itself as inbound, and the maintenance-workspace copy was also missing the v2.5.20 doubly-wrapped-envelope fallback. **Seeing the same names is not deciding the same way.** The decision is now one delimited block (`§13.16.9 CLASSIFY BEGIN`…`END`) required to be byte-identical across copies — a differing comment line fails, which is the intent — and the checker additionally requires each regression guard to still be present inside it, because identical copies can still be identically wrong. The MCP `MEANINGFUL` set stays a declared exception: it filters a history view, not a wake path, and a view has no turn to interrupt. `§13.16.9-a`; parity checker 24 → 33 assertions; the replay instrument is kept as `scripts/measure-meaningful-inversion.cjs` (read-only, extracts the allowlist from the canonical probe at runtime rather than becoming a fifth copy of it).

- **v2.6.29** (2026-07-27) — **One dependency the adopter was told to install; another the platform already had** — Plugins are distributed as a code copy with no install step, so every npm dependency they declare is absent in the only configuration adopters run. Two declared parts, two different correct answers. `ws`: the MCP server refused to connect without it, while the reference clients in the same repository declared nothing and worked — all 10 of their connect sites use the **built-in global `WebSocket`** that Node has provided since 22. The server's module scope held `let WebSocket = null`, which **shadowed that global**, so the part the runtime already had was unreachable by name; one declaration hid a working transport and manufactured an install step for every adopter. Fixed by using the platform part, with `ws` demoted to `optionalDependencies` behind `engines.node >= 22` for runtimes that lack the global. Carrying a copy instead would have added ~129KB and made this repository responsible for tracking advisories in a component the platform patches on its own. `ajv`: no platform equivalent exists, so it is now **carried in-tree** — generated from `plugins/hyperbrief/vendor.manifest.json` by `scripts/sync-vendored-deps.mjs`, never hand-maintained, because a derived copy lags with no signal and the symptom is a plausible wrong conclusion rather than an error. The tree is pruned by what a runtime *cannot load* — type declarations, source maps, TypeScript sources, tests, benchmarks, CI config — and keeps **every** `.js`/`.json`/license file including paths this module never takes: 173 files / 430KB, from 546 / 1351KB unpruned. Deliberately **not** pruned to the measured require-closure (88 files / 257KB), because a tree tuned to the paths this repository exercises breaks the first adopter who takes another one. Licenses (MIT ×4 + BSD-3-Clause) retained in place with a generated `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md` the checker keeps in sync. The general invariant is now machine-checked across every plugin: **`dependencies` is a promise about the shipped tree** — declare it required and it must resolve there; carry it or move it to `optionalDependencies` behind a platform fallback or a refusal that names the part. Declaring required-and-unshipped is the false marker this whole class started from. Validation is asserted end-to-end in the shipped layout — the checker calls the tool as a host would and requires `skipped: false` plus a response that *changes when the input changes*, because "the file is present" is not the claim "validation ran". Its first run is the argument for it: the three decision briefs emitted the day before had gone out unvalidated, and turning validation on reported **36 violations across them**, including a sentence where the schema requires an integer and strings where objects are required. A hand-written check had passed those same IRs, because it was written from the same reading of §2 that produced them — **a check derived from the author's understanding re-derives the author's mistakes.** Two module-side gaps are recorded rather than excused: §2 names the `coupling_delta` fields without stating their types, and `trigger_phrases_md` requires an array despite its `_md` suffix. One defect this cut introduced and caught before shipping: adapting the EventEmitter call sites to the WHATWG surface surfaced connect failures as an `AggregateError` with an empty `message`, so a dead endpoint answered `{"code": -32603, "message": ""}` — and the first version of the new assertion ("the message must not be a part-absence refusal") **passed** on it, because an empty string matches no pattern. An error with no content is the same defect shape as a success that renders nothing. The cause chain is now flattened into the message with the endpoint origin (query string dropped — the auth key travels there), and the assertion asks what a failure *says* before asking what it is not. Constellation `§13.27.7` (transport parts) + Hyperbrief `§11.6` (the carried validator); checkers 17 → 18, one new (`verify-vendored-deps`, 23 assertions) and `verify-optional-dep-honesty` extended to `optionalDependencies` with the shipped-tree invariant.

- **v2.6.28** (2026-07-27) — **A discipline written down fourteen times still failed, so it was replaced with a shape and a hook (Greatpractice v0.3.5)**  — The workspace rule "use absolute paths, the shell's directory persists between calls" has been recorded, followed, and broken repeatedly — fourteen occurrences across three coordinates. The first two coordinates announce themselves: a relative path points at nothing and the command errors, or a long-lived process carries a stale `PATH` and a freshly installed tool reads as missing. Those cost a retry. The third coordinate, measured this session, **succeeds**: with two overlapping repositories that both have stageable changes, committing in the wrong one is an ordinary successful commit. A release commit carrying the nested public repo's message convention landed in the private outer repo, a version tag was created and pushed to the wrong remote, and the intended changes stayed uncommitted — so the next cut's edits landed on the same files and the two releases could no longer be separated. Nothing in the tool output indicated a problem; the only signal came from an unrelated check asserting that every changelog release marker has a tag. That asymmetry is the whole argument for changing shape rather than trying harder. `cd` sets state that outlives the command, so every later invocation inherits a decision made earlier and a chain that fails midway leaves the wrong state for whatever runs next. `git -C <absolute>` re-establishes the target on every call and cannot be inherited. And where the wrong target is *also valid*, care produces no signal at all, so the signal has to be manufactured: a `commit-msg` hook in the repository that must not receive a given commit shape, rejecting the other repository's release-message convention and printing the correct `git -C` invocation. It encodes one stable fact — these two repositories have different commit conventions, so a message in the other's format is evidence of a misroute — and infers nothing else. Verified in both directions before installing: the wrong shape is rejected with the correct route, the local convention passes. Ratified as the tenth mezzo entry, `nested-repo-write-routing`, at `recommended` rather than `mandatory`: the rule is about **writes**, and banning `cd` outright would penalize ordinary exploration. It generalizes past git — editing a deployment copy instead of the source master, writing to a board on the wrong port, patching a plugin cache instead of the repository are the same shape, and the statement is that when two valid targets exist the command must name one. Prevention and detection stay separate jobs here, which is why the changelog-marker-to-tag check is named in the entry rather than replaced by it.
- **v2.6.27** (2026-07-27) — **The local join path had a reference client and the collab path did not, so an adopter built one and missed five contracts at once (Constellation v2.4.107)**  — `join-local.cjs` was the reference for the local-worker join path and there was no counterpart for collab / peer join, so an adopter built one from the spec alone. It missed five protocol contracts, each of which produced a measured incident, and two of those incidents landed on this board rather than theirs. No `AckProcessed`: every targeted message addressed to them was redelivered three times and closed as `RelayUnreachable{commitment-ack-absent}` — they received the messages, the senders recorded non-delivery, and nothing in their own logs said anything was wrong. HELLO without `clientId`/`agentName`/`protocolVersion`/`capabilities`: accepted as a connection, never registered as a participant. `AgentHello` omitted **deliberately**, because this spec's "no rebroadcast noise" wording was read as forbidding it — a sentence that can be read as its own opposite has failed, and that is a defect in the sentence. No single-instance guard: the spawning shell died, the node child was orphaned, and several instances of one `agentId` kicked each other about once a second. `History` appended verbatim to their store: the board replays the full history on every reconnect, so the store multiplied by connection generation — 594 MB, 1,414 of 1,425 lines being `History`, past the point their tooling could read the file. The fourth one is the sharpest. `single-instance.cjs` has documented that exact runaway in this repository since 2026-06-07, including the consequence chain down to a usage-policy block. The lesson was written down, shipped, and still did not reach the adopter — because the only file that reaches for it is the *local* join path. A guard that exists but sits behind a door adopters do not open is not a shipped guard, and the missing reference was the door. So the new client is not an invention: contracts 1–4 are carried from `join-local.cjs` unchanged, and it exists so the collab surface has the floor the local surface already had. Three additions come from the adopter's request plus measurement here. The send path **drains an outbox file over the resident connection** — a client that opens a socket per send kicks its own resident listener, and the fixed-delay send that follows goes out over a dead socket and vanishes silently. The store **excludes metadata by name**, so the `History` multiplication cannot recur. And **delivery-failure notices are surfaced by default**, to a separate file and to stderr; that is the general form of the adopter's own request and the mirror of the gap two cuts earlier where 22 `RelayUnreachable` notices sat unread on this board. Orphan avoidance is stated precisely because the obvious implementation is wrong: the client does **not** infer abandonment from whether its parent is alive. A shell pipeline's intermediate process exits first, so a healthy child sees a dead parent — measured on Windows during this same investigation, where that inference produced a false accusation against an unrelated process and a recommendation to kill it. The spawner passes its own pid as `PARENT_PID`; when it is absent the client says at startup that the protection is off rather than pretending to have it. Verified by `scripts/smoke-join-collab.cjs` — 19 assertions against an isolated board with an observing peer reading the wire, registered in the single verify entry point. The load-bearing assertion: `AgentList` arrives four times and `AgentHello` is still sent once. Removing the guard makes the count follow `AgentList` (1 → 4), which is the flood in miniature, and the assertion fails — the regression is defended directly rather than by inspection. One assertion had to be repaired while writing it: on an empty board no `History` is ever sent, so "the store excludes History bodies" passed while observing nothing, and the fixture now seeds history before the client connects.
- **v2.6.26** (2026-07-27) — **The previous cut left candidates on the table, and inside the same session that cost a real message (Constellation v2.4.106)**  — One cut earlier, four names were added to the §13.16.9 meaningful-inbound allowlist on measured evidence and the remaining observations were noted as candidates. `SpecGapReport` was one of the candidates — 11 occurrences on the wire, from two different adopters. Within the same session an adopter sent a product proposal under that name, and the turn-end probe answered "nothing meaningful" while the proposal sat unprocessed in the inbox, alongside four earlier reports from the same family that had never surfaced either. An incomplete fix bites in exactly the place the original defect did, and it bites sooner, because the evidence was already in hand and set aside. Six names are added here, each carrying a stated reason rather than a position in a list: `SpecGapReport` / `SpecGapCode` (an adopter telling you your spec is wrong, plus the code that shows it), `Proposal`, `ReturnPackage` (a delegated deliverable coming back), `PhaseBScopeShare`, `TaskEnvelope`. The measurement that produced those six also produced something the list cannot absorb. One observed name is `AdopterFeedback-MangoTalk-20260720` — an adopter minted a **date-stamped, single-use intent name**. No enumerated allowlist can cover names invented by other parties, which means that for agent-authored envelopes addressed to a specific recipient the allowlist has the wrong shape: filtering by known-good names silently drops everything new, and an unlisted name is indistinguishable from an absent message. That is the same failure signature this axis has produced twice in two cuts. The candidate correction inverts the default for agent-authored **and** targeted envelopes — surface unless denylisted as transport or telemetry, keeping the enumeration as the classification of noise rather than the definition of signal. Inverting it changes what wakes an agent for every adopter, so it is written into the spec as an open decision with its evidence and deliberately not applied in this cut. The parity checker's minimum set now carries the six with their reasons. Copy-equality alone cannot catch a name disappearing from all four copies at once — it would report agreement, which is the failure mode of every check in this family. 24 assertions, and reverting one copy still fails it with the absent names listed.
- **v2.6.25** (2026-07-27) — **The server had been reporting our undelivered messages all along, and the filter classified that as not meaningful (Constellation v2.4.105)**  — An adopter reported that a reply of ours had never arrived and traced it to their own client never sending the commitment-tier `AckProcessed`, which is true and was their gap. It was only half. The server had emitted `RelayUnreachable{msgId, targetAgentId, attemptCount, lastError}` into our inbox at the time, and it sat there unread — because `RelayUnreachable` was not in the §13.16.9 meaningful-inbound allowlist, so neither the turn-end probe nor the low-latency watcher ever surfaced it. 22 non-deliveries had accumulated that way. Notice of your own outbound never landing is the single most actionable inbound there is, and it was being filtered as noise; a non-delivery notice nobody reads is indistinguishable from delivery. The loop was closed by the counterparty telling us, not by the signal that had been sitting in the inbox — which is the part worth recording, because two blind spots multiplied and both ends believed the message was sent. Three more names were missing for the same reason and are added on measured evidence, not intuition. `SelectionPrompt` — a choice being asked of you. `SelectionExpired` — a choice you asked that expired unanswered. `Response` — the reply half of the generic `Request` envelope, which matters because `Reply` **was** allowlisted while measured wire traffic carries `Response` and never `Reply`. A guard standing in front of a name nobody sends reads exactly like a working guard, which is the same shape as the rest of this: the absence of a complaint looked like success. The set turned out to exist in four copies — the canonical stop-hook probe, the plugin's shipped copy, the plugin MCP server's own `MEANINGFUL`, and the workspace's manual probe — and the manual copy was already six names behind. The consequence was quiet and worse for being quiet: reading the same inbox, the manual pre-send probe was **less sensitive than the turn-end probe**, so the same message could be meaningful at one gate and invisible at the other with nothing erroring. The three probe copies are now identical and asserted so. The MCP server's set is deliberately left alone: its consumer is history-tail rather than a turn gate, its two membership differences may well be intentional, and there was no way to establish that from here — so it is registered as an exception with a stated reason that prints on every run rather than quietly normalized into agreement. Guessing at intent and calling it a fix is how a real distinction gets erased. Verified by `scripts/verify-meaningful-set-parity.cjs` — 18 assertions, registered in the single verify entry point. It asserts the three probe copies are byte-equal as sets, that a minimum set carrying a stated reason per name is present in all four, and that the comparator detects both a missing name and an extra one. Reverting a single copy fails it with the ten absent names listed by name. The minimum set is deliberately a reason-annotated set rather than a list: a list that grew without reasons is one a later reader can neither prune nor extend.
- **v2.6.24** (2026-07-27) — **A validation that never ran reported `ok: true`, and a dependency nobody called was still advertised (Hyperbrief v0.7.4 · Ultrasafe v0.2.7)**  — Fixing the response envelope one cut earlier made the tool output visible, and the first thing it showed was a second defect the invisibility had been covering: `hyperbrief_validate` answered `ok: true` when `ajv` was absent. It did disclose — `skipped: true` and a `reason` rode along — but the field a caller gates on is `ok`, so an IR that was never checked read as valid. The correct behavior already existed in this repository as a control: the board tools refuse when `ws` is missing and name the package in the message. Being unable to do the work is forgivable; not saying so is not, and a green verdict is the loudest way of not saying so. `hyperbrief_validate` now refuses, naming the package and the directory to install it in, and no longer reports a verdict it did not compute. The measurement that surfaced it also drew the real boundary, which is wider than one tool. Plugins are distributed as a code copy with no install step, so **every declared npm dependency is absent in the only configuration an adopter runs** — 3 declarations across the module set, 0 `node_modules` anywhere, in the source tree as well as the installed one. Two of the three now behave correctly under absence. The renderer was already honest and needed no change: both of its validate call sites push a skip warning into the returned `warnings`, so an unvalidated render announces itself rather than passing as a validated one. That honest behavior is now asserted rather than assumed, because nothing was holding it in place. Ultrasafe declared `ajv` and never called it. The validator factory had no call sites at all and the `../schemas/` directory it resolved against does not exist — so the declaration bought a free signal ("this module validates against schemas") for a capability that had no schemas, no callers, and no way to run. That is a false marker, not a latent feature, so it is removed rather than wired up; if schema validation is wanted later, the validator, the schemas and the call sites belong in one cut. Eviction has a documentation tail and paying it is the point: five surfaces asserted the removed thing (`Single npm dep (ajv)`, `the validator gracefully skips when absent`, a dependency comment in the §14 file tree, the §16.6 code sketch, and the docs page), and all five are corrected in this cut. A standard that cannot prune its own claims becomes the burden its successor has to carry. Verified by `scripts/verify-optional-dep-honesty.cjs` — 12 assertions, registered in the single verify entry point. It walks every plugin `package.json`, asserts each declared dependency is actually `require`d somewhere in that package (a declaration with no call site fails the build), and for each dependency that is genuinely absent it drives the server over stdio and asserts the absence is reported as a refusal naming the package rather than as a success. Unobservable is counted as SKIP, never as pass — if a dependency turns out to be installed, the absence path cannot be exercised and the run says so instead of quietly counting a win. Two checker defects were found and fixed while writing it, both of the same shape it exists to catch: it counted a function definition and a code comment as call sites and failed a correct file, and its `ok: true` assertion passed on a reverted tree because the payload sits inside the envelope's text item where the quotes are escaped. The negative test now fails two assertions on the reverted tree, and the dead-declaration detector proves itself in the same run by catching a deliberately planted unused dependency.
- **v2.6.23** (2026-07-26) — **Three of the four tool servers answered with nothing to render, and the tools themselves were fine (Compendium v0.2.10 · Hyperbrief v0.7.3 · Ultrasafe v0.2.6)**  — The vocabulary tools stayed silent after the previous cut corrected the store path and every layer of the plugin install was confirmed against the new build — which is what made the second defect visible: `tools/call` was returning the handler's result object directly, with no `content` array. That is not a protocol error. It is a valid success carrying nothing a host can render, so the call reports no output and the tool looks **absent** rather than broken, which sends the diagnosis to the wrong layer every time. Measured across the four servers: compendium, hyperbrief and ultrasafe returned bare objects; constellation wrapped correctly, and being able to call a sibling that answered *with* a visible error is what separated "the transport is dead" from "the shape is wrong." Both layers were real, and that is the part worth recording. The earlier note on this symptom had narrowed it to the transport layer; that note was overwritten once the store path was proven, and the store path turned out to be only the first of two. A proven cause is not the only cause — the record should have gained a layer instead of replacing one, because the first defect was hiding the second. The envelope is applied at **one dispatch choke point per server**, not per tool. Per-tool wrapping is exactly how this spread: a handler added later omits it and only that tool goes quiet, which is the same objection that put the store assertion at a single choke point one cut earlier. Pass-through is idempotent, so a handler already returning a shaped envelope is untouched and the compliant server needed no change at all. Ultrasafe's CLI surface deliberately keeps the unwrapped result — the envelope is a protocol concern, and a human reading CLI output should not receive JSON nested inside a JSON envelope. `structuredContent` is deliberately **not** added: these servers advertise protocol version `2024-11-05`, which predates it, and shipping a field from a later revision while claiming the earlier one invites a client to validate against a contract the server is not offering. It is a named follow-on for whenever the advertised version moves. Verified by `scripts/smoke-mcp-envelope.cjs` — 24 assertions, registered in the single verify entry point. It spawns each **declared** server over stdio exactly as a host does rather than requiring the module, because the require surface is precisely where a protocol-layer defect is invisible. The server registry is cross-checked in both directions — declared but absent, present on disk but undeclared — and every declared server must have a read-only probe defined, so adding a server without one fails the build instead of being skipped. Envelope validation rejects empty `content` arrays and non-string text, so it cannot pass for the wrong reason, which was the failure shape of the guard this replaces. It also proves it can fail in the same run it passes: it writes a deliberately non-compliant server, drives it through the same code path, and asserts the validator rejects it. On a reverted tree the two content assertions fail with the exact diagnosis.
- **v2.6.22** (2026-07-26) — **The vocabulary module was completely non-functional when installed, and said nothing about it (Compendium v0.2.9)**  — Found while verifying that a plugin refresh had taken effect: with the new build finally running, `wiki_search` returned nothing. The store was located by walking two directories up from the runtime's own file — correct inside the source repo, where `plugins/compendium/` sits beside `compendium/`, and wrong in the only configuration an adopter ever runs. Installed as a plugin, two levels up is the directory holding the plugin's **own version folders** (`0.2.1` / `0.2.6` / `0.2.8`), so the store had no entries and every tool answered empty. The module had been shipped broken for its entire intended audience while passing all of its own lints, because the lints run in-repo. **The silence is the part worth fixing, not the wrong path.** That directory exists, so the existence guard passed; only `glossary/` · `concept/` · `runbook/` were absent, and an absent subdirectory is skipped rather than reported. Zero entries, no error, nothing anywhere saying why — a check that passed for the wrong reason, producing an answer indistinguishable from *"nothing matched."* Two rules replace it. **A store is recognized by its contents, never by its directory existing**: validation requires `index.json`, `INDEX.md`, or at least one `.md` under a declared subdirectory, which would have rejected the wrong path on the first call instead of answering quietly for weeks. **An unresolved store is a refusal, not an empty result**: the tools now raise an error naming `COMPENDIUM_STORE` and listing every location tried, because silence gives the operator nothing to act on while a refusal that says where it looked is repairable in one step. Resolution order, with the reason for each rung: `COMPENDIUM_STORE` first — explicit intent outranks inference, and if it is set and invalid resolution **stops** rather than falling through, since quietly reading a *different* vocabulary is worse than reading none (the answers look right); then module-relative, preserved byte-for-byte so the release verifier's pointer-resolution axis is unchanged; then `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` and cwd walked upward, each root checked at itself **and one level down**, because a public repo nested inside a maintenance workspace is a common layout and checking only the root misses it. More than one valid store under a root refuses and names them rather than picking — an arbitrary choice among vocabularies cannot be explained afterward. The MCP surface asserts resolution at a single dispatch choke point rather than per tool, so a tool added later cannot quietly reintroduce the empty answer. Board correction worth recording: the tracked item had this narrowed to "the transport layer, not the tool," which was wrong and would have sent the next attempt to the wrong layer. Verified by `scripts/verify-compendium-store-resolve.cjs` — 11 assertions including the installed-plugin layout, which reproduces the silent empty result on a reverted tree. Takes effect for this deployment only after the plugin is refreshed again.
- **v2.6.21** (2026-07-26) — **The lifetime is finally asked about, and the renewal path survived it (Constellation v2.4.104)**  — The second half of the ordering the previous cut set up: enforcement, taken only after every lapsed key on the deployment had been renewed, so it disconnected nobody. Three things it holds. **Both admission sites, tested separately.** A presented key is resolved at the connection upgrade (query-string keys) and at HELLO (body keys); v2.4.101 is the record of patching one and testing with an input that carried the key in both, so the fix passed and did nothing live because the reference worker keys itself through the URL alone. One shared predicate is now called from both, and the smoke exercises URL-only and body-only as distinct assertions. **The upgrade refusal precedes the board payload.** A URL-keyed client receives `SERVER_HELLO`, `AgentList` and `History` before it ever sends HELLO, so refusing at HELLO time refuses *after* the handover — the check goes ahead of those sends, the same ordering v2.4.41 established for address-blocked connections, and the smoke asserts a refused connection received none of the three. **Refusal must not consume the renewal path.** Expiring writes the lapse into stored state so the read-time view and the record stop disagreeing, but it must not set `revokedAt` — that field means *an operator ended this key* and is the one condition renewal refuses. Recording expiry as revocation would make every aged-out key permanently unrenewable, silently, and discovered only by an operator trying and failing to fix an outage the enforcement itself caused; the asymmetry that made this feature safe has to survive the feature that consumes it, so it is asserted directly rather than left to follow from careful coding. `ConnectionRejected` carries `code: 'key-expired'` with the key's label and expiry instant, because an operator reading a counterparty's report needs to know which key to renew and that renewal — not re-issuance — is the remedy. `ttl: 0` keys, including everything adopted from the legacy store, are untouched: giving them a lifetime is a separate decision, not a side effect. On the deployment itself the three lapsed keys were renewed first (14 days each, same key strings, nothing re-delivered) and only then was this cut applied. Verified by `scripts/smoke-key-ttl-enforce.cjs` — 12 assertions, 5 failing on a pre-enforcement tree.
- **v2.6.20** (2026-07-26) — **Enforcing a lifetime nobody could renew would have been an outage (Constellation v2.4.103)**  — Every key declares a 14-day lifetime that the admission path never consults, so expired credentials keep working while the management view already calls them revoked. The fix is small; the decision was not, because of what turning it on does. Measured on this deployment, three keys were already past their window — the board's own worker at 35 days and two collaborating projects — so a correct security change would have arrived as a simultaneous three-way disconnection. The operator's call was to build the renewal path first. This cut is that path; enforcement is a separate step, taken once no live key is lapsed, so that it cuts nobody. **Expiry derives from the current window, not from issuance.** `renewedAt` opens a new window and `issuedAt` stays immutable — when a credential first came into existence is a fact worth keeping, and a renewal that overwrote it would destroy the ability to ask how long a key has been in circulation. Which means a consumer recomputing `issuedAt + ttl` is **wrong** on any renewed key, so `expiresAt` now rides on `KeyIssued` / `KeyList` / `KeyRenewed` rather than being left to be derived, and the dashboard reads it instead of recalculating — a derived copy that silently disagrees with its source is the failure class this contract is trying not to add to. **Renewal restarts the window and does not change the key string.** Nobody receives a new secret, reconfigures anything, or is told to reconnect — which is exactly the cost that made bare enforcement the wrong first move, since re-issuing would have required a human to carry a new credential to another project and left that project disconnected until they did. **The asymmetry is the whole security content.** A key that lapsed by TTL alone may be renewed; a key an operator explicitly revoked may not, ever. Both read as `REVOKED` through the effective-state view, so `KeyList` now carries `lapsed` and `revokedAt` and consumers branch on the *cause* rather than on the rendered state. Collapsing them would make revocation mean "revoked until someone clicks renew" — a worse defect than the unenforced TTL this work exists to make enforceable. The key modal offers only the actions the wire will honor for each cause, because a button that produces a refusal teaches the operator to distrust the surface. **A credential you cannot address is a credential you cannot manage.** `local`-kind keys never appear in wire responses by design (§3.6) and every canonical verb took the key string as its selector, so those keys could not be renewed, revoked, or relabelled from the management surface at all — the same *valid but unmanageable* class v2.4.87 closed for legacy-file keys, left open for one kind. Not hypothetical: the 35-day-lapsed key is exactly that kind. Keys now carry `keyRef`, a random non-secret stable handle every management verb accepts as an alternative selector, assigned in one place (the persist path) so a new call site cannot forget it. `KeyRenew` sits inside the §13.25.9 operator gate — a verb that mutates credential lifetime must not be reachable by a non-main agent connection, and the smoke asserts that refusal rather than assuming it. **Warning is part of the path, not a courtesy**, since being able to renew does not help an operator who learns of an expiry from a broken connection: an interval sweep surfaces each key inside a 3-day window on three surfaces — the server log, a server-attributed board announcement that persists in history, and a direct notice to a live holder so a collaborating project can ask for its own renewal — capped at once per key per day, because a warning that repeats every sweep is a warning nobody reads. Deliberately **not** done: the main agent is not woken. An expiry warning is a notice, and §13.16.9's four-group classification puts notices outside the waking set; adding this one intent because it feels important is how that classification stops meaning anything. Verified by `scripts/smoke-key-renewal.cjs` — 22 assertions, 18 of them failing on a reverted tree — and registered in `verify-all.cjs`.
- **v2.6.19** (2026-07-26) — **The counter had no writer, and the key found nothing (Ultrasafe v0.2.5)**  — Two coupled defects the security pass found in its own machinery, fixed together because the first depends on the second. **The counter had no writer.** `.ultrasafe/state.json` carried 60+ detection events with `"iterations": []`: the PreToolUse hook only appends events, the Stop hook only *reads* `state.iterations`, and the MCP server never touched the file at all. So the v0.3 blocking-mode criterion "advisory evidence has accumulated per release" read as **satisfied** — and was reported that way to the operator — while the count had never moved once. `ultrasafe_iteration_record` is the missing writer. It follows the **consumer's** contract rather than inventing one: the four fields the Stop hook's AND-gate actually reads (`open_findings`, `new_findings_above_threshold`, `coverage`, `clean`), with the state path resolved by **byte-identical** anchoring logic to the hook's, since a writer and reader that disagree about which file they mean reproduce this exact silence. Three deliberate choices: `clean` is **derived** (new-above-threshold zero AND coverage at floor) and never accepted as a caller declaration, because optimistic self-report is how a gate passes without being met; when the previous iteration stored no key set the new-finding count is **`null`, not `0`**, because zero asserts *no regression* and that assertion would be the same false confidence in a new place; and if the state file is absent the tool **refuses rather than creating one**, since a second file at a mismatched anchor is the measured cwd-split-history incident. **The key found nothing.** Exact `file × line × pattern_id` dedup produced **zero** cross-axis matches across 52 findings, from two causes. Agents reported paths against different bases — normalization closes that. The worse one was the **line number in the key**: edit any line and every finding in that file gets a new key, so `new_findings_above_threshold` can never reach zero and `regression_free` stays false regardless of real progress — the gate reads improvement as regression. The key is now normalized-path × pattern_id × title-fingerprint, line-insensitive, with the fingerprint present so two distinct findings sharing a pattern in one file do not merge (undercounting makes the gate *easier*, which is the wrong direction to err). Stated because it would otherwise be assumed closed: **semantic duplicates with different titles still do not merge.** One defect seen from two call sites is beyond a mechanical key, exactly as iteration 1 reported. What is fixed is the path-base cause entirely and the line-churn cause entirely. Both key sites in the server now share one function; they had drifted into two copies of the same broken 3-tuple. And **iteration 1 is now recorded** — retroactively, from the same findings on disk, with every number read rather than restated: 52 findings, severity split critical 8 / high 10 / medium 14 / low 8 / info 12 (independently matching the report), coverage 7 attackers against 13 declared axes = 0.54 which is **below** the 0.8 floor, so `clean: false`. That is not a defect; it is what this iteration was. The gate now says `iterations_run: 1` against a requirement of ≥ 3 — honestly, and for the first time. Verified by `scripts/verify-ultrasafe-iteration.cjs`, 17 assertions, which redirects the state file to a sandbox and **asserts the redirection took effect before writing anything** — a checker that quietly wrote to the live history would fabricate precisely the evidence whose absence it exists to detect.
- **v2.6.18** (2026-07-26) — **A fix you cannot observe on your platform has not been shown to work there (Constellation v2.4.102)**  — A one-paragraph correction to the at-rest hardening, worth its own entry because the alternative is an adopter drawing the wrong conclusion from a correct measurement. The previous cut hardens five secret paths and the local-key directory to `0600`/`0700` at startup and on every write. On Windows that is close to a no-op: `fs.chmod` toggles only the read-only bit and cannot express owner-only, so a file **created** with `mode: 0o600` reads back as `0666`. That was probed on the deployment rather than assumed, after the modes came back unchanged from a restart and the first reading was "the fix did not take". It did take; the platform cannot show it. §13.25.11 now says so, in both directions — an operator seeing `0666` there must not conclude the patch failed, and equally must not conclude the files are protected, because on that platform the protection has to come from the filesystem ACLs instead. The reference smoke test encodes the same split: the hardening **code path** is asserted by its log line on every platform, while the resulting **mode** is asserted only where the platform can represent it and reports not-run elsewhere. Calling that a pass would be the worse of the two available lies.
- **v2.6.17** (2026-07-26) — **The fix passed its own test and did not work on the live board (Constellation v2.4.101)**  — Restarting the deployment to activate the two previous cuts produced two measurements that contradicted their tests, and both failures are the same shape: **the test exercised a path the real client does not use.** First — the worker's key still read `state: ISSUED`, `lastAgent: null` after reconnecting, exactly as before the fix that was supposed to start observing it. The kind of a presented key is resolved at **two** places, the connection upgrade (for a key in the query string) and the `HELLO` handler (for a key in the message body), and the earlier cut added the missing `local` branch to only the second one. The reference local worker keys itself **through the URL only** — so its key was still never observed, and, more seriously, the remote-`local`-key refusal never fired for it either. The smoke test had passed because it sent the key in *both* places, which is not what any real client does; it now keys the worker case through the URL alone and adds an explicit URL-only remote case. One assertion is worth recording for what it says about the design: on the unfixed tree the URL-only forger still failed to obtain `main`, because the host-locality guard held even with the kind branch missing. That is the layering doing its job — no single guard is load-bearing — and it is the reason this gap was a missed hardening rather than an open takeover. Second — every secret file on disk was still at its old mode after the restart. The previous cut set `0600` on the **write** path, and these files are written only when keys change, so an existing deployment stays world-readable until the next key operation, which may be never. The finding had said this in a clause easy to skim past ("on first run, **also** chmod, in case an earlier laxer-mode version already exists"), and skimming it is what happened. The server now hardens the five secret paths plus the `local-keys/` directory **at startup**, so the fix applies to files that already exist rather than only to files it creates. Neither of these was found by reasoning about the diff; both came from restarting and then reading the state, which is the discipline this project already writes down as *completion is judged by state measurement, never by a transport ack* — applied here to a security patch rather than to a delegation.
- **v2.6.16** (2026-07-26) — **A defect nobody can diff is a defect nobody reviews (Constellation v2.4.100, Compendium v0.2.8)**  — The remaining ranked items from the security pass, plus two findings the audit's own instruction produced. The pass ranked *private key material persisted with no restrictive file mode* as **critical**, and this cut had it filed lower — corrected by reading the finding rather than the summary. Five files hold secrets and all five relied entirely on the process umask, which under the common POSIX default yields **world-readable** `0644`: the VAPID private JWK including its private scalar, the push-subscription tokens, the raw A2A key registry, the key store, and each local worker's key file. All five now write at `0600`, and each write is followed by a defensive `chmod` — because `mode` applies **only at file creation**, so overwriting a file that already exists with wider permissions silently keeps them, which is exactly how a "fixed" permission bug survives a deploy. The `local-keys/` directory drops to `0700` as well: it was `0755`, and since a label *is* the key's filename, a listable directory handed over the labels too. Neither that directory nor those key files were in the finding — they came from following its instruction to sweep the same class, which is the difference between closing a finding and closing a defect. On the vocabulary store's MCP server, the traversal fix (**high**) went in as the finding specified, mirroring the correct implementation already shipped in a sibling plugin: a strict slug pattern **and** a resolve-then-compare boundary check, both, because the pattern constrains the shape and the boundary check constrains the result. The audit also asked for the same sweep across every tool that builds a path from a call argument, which surfaced the read-side twin — `owner_spec`'s file component is caller-supplied too and reached a read with no boundary check. Verified with hostile arguments driven through the real functions (traversal, absolute, separator injection, backslash, NUL truncation, uppercase/space) plus the assertion that all **34** existing entry slugs still pass, since a guard that also rejects legitimate input is a different outage rather than a fix. And the finding that was not in any report: the store's server carried a **literal NUL byte** in a search separator. Its intent is defensible — a byte that cannot occur in content cannot produce a cross-field false match — but as a raw byte in source it made **git classify the entire file as binary**, so from the file's first commit every change to it reported as `-	-` in numstat and **no line-level diff was ever reviewable**. Escaping it preserves the runtime behavior exactly and returns the file to the tools people review with. This is the session's recurring shape at a third address: the tool did not error, it went quiet, and quiet read as fine. The same file also could not be *tested*, because requiring it attached a stdin listener — so the stdio loop is now entrypoint-guarded and the tool implementations are exported for checkers; the protocol surface when a host runs it is unchanged. Two new verifiers ship with this: `scripts/verify-mcp-path-guard.cjs` (9 assertions, 2 failing on a reverted copy) and the NUL-byte invariant asserted on the working file rather than on a diff against HEAD — a diff was the wrong probe, since while the committed blob still holds the NUL git reports binary because *one side* is binary, and the check would have failed after the fix and then passed for an unrelated reason. When a tool cannot reach what it audits it reports **not-run**, never pass: on the reverted copy the traversal assertions could not execute at all, and that is what they said.
- **v2.6.15** (2026-07-26) — **The invariant said identity binds by declaration. Nothing checked that the declaration was true (Constellation v2.4.99)**  — Yesterday's cut shipped §13.30.9, whose load-bearing rule is that *identity binds by declaration, never by resemblance*. A security pass over the shipped runtime found the rule was sound and its precondition was missing: the wire had **no relationship between the identity a connection claimed and the credential it presented**, so the resolution ladder worked exactly as written and resolved, correctly and precisely, onto a forger. The invariant was not wrong; it was **incomplete**. **§13.25.11** supplies the missing layer — *a declaration must be authenticated before it can be bound* — and this entry states the chain plainly because it was **reproduced end to end**, not inferred: against a pre-fix copy of the reference, a remote party holding one `local`-kind key takes the operating main's station and the real main's socket closes; against the fixed copy every step after the first is refused. Four steps, each cheap. **Reconnaissance was free**: the main's id is printed in onboarding text, and the `local` onboarding endpoint was gated by a *label* instead of a key while also being excluded from the address allowlist along with the rest of `/join/*` — an exclusion written for its key-gated siblings — so an unauthenticated remote caller who guessed a worker label was handed the main's id and that worker's role description (measured live: 200, 4.6 KB, id present twice). **The privilege step was a string comparison**: `main` resolved from bare equality between the claimed id and the configured primary id, and `main` is also the operator predicate — key issuance, revocation, handover, organization authorship — so one claim crossed the entire authority boundary. **Only one kind of key could reach it**: `collab`/`peer`/`upstream` keys set a role flag that pins the connection off the main branch; a `local` key set none, and nothing required a credential meaning *host-local* to be presented from the host it names. **And it was takeover, not coexistence**: registering an id evicts the connection already holding it. The fixes are layered so that no single one is load-bearing: `main` is a **host-local station** and a remote connection does not resolve to it whatever it declares (the supported remote counterpart is the `peer` kind, which never reaches that branch); a `local`-kind key is **refused from a non-local address**; keys **bind to an identity on first use** and a later connection claiming a different identity with the same key is refused with a stable machine-readable `code` in the `ConnectionRejected` body — previously the code existed only in the close frame, leaving adopters to match prose; the envelope's `agentId` is **overwritten** from the authenticated connection rather than filled when absent, because a present-but-forged value was passing unchecked and persisting into board history; an agent connection may no longer claim `source: 'server'`, which is what let any sender forge a system-authoritative announcement — the field's own comment said "client-set wins", so `source_stamp_truth` was never truth; and `/join/local` is host-local. Two surfaces beyond identity: state-changing POSTs now additionally require same-origin browser signals, because a loopback-only check is satisfied by a browser on the same machine no matter which page's script fired the request — any page the operator visited could rewrite the access policy and then trigger a restart to apply it, turning "secure-by-default loopback bind" into an unauthenticated key-management surface; and the board-state stream stops answering `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, which with the previous item let a third-party page both read and rewrite the board. One fix is a **hollow counter** of the kind promoted to durable discipline this morning: `local`-kind keys were never *observed*, because the branch that records a key's identity and lifecycle only ran for the three remote kinds — so a worker connected for weeks showed `state: ISSUED`, `lastAgent: null`, `connectionStatus: never`. There was a reader and no writer, and the dashboard reported the initial value as a fact. Verification is `scripts/smoke-auth-binding.cjs`: 20 assertions against an isolated server, of which **12 fail on a reverted tree** — including the takeover itself, asserted as *the real main still holds the station*. The remote-path assertions report **SKIP, never PASS**, when the host has no non-loopback address, because a silent skip that reads as a pass is the exact failure this file exists to prevent. Two gaps are recorded and deliberately **not** closed. Disclosure already relayed is **not retractable**: when the declared main is absent the server elects the first live agent for target-unspecified traffic, and §13.13.3 widened that traffic three cuts ago, so the window leaks more than it did — it self-heals on reconnect, but nothing un-relays. And **a declared TTL that is never consulted is not a TTL**: the key model declares a 14-day default and the read path already reports expired keys as revoked, but the authorization checkpoint never asked, so the management surface and the wire disagree. Enforcing it is correct and is not bundled here, because on the reference deployment it would disconnect **three keys in one step without warning** — one of them a local worker's, expired 34 days — so it needs a renewal path and an operator decision, not a patch. Recording a gap while declining to close it is the honest order; the alternative is a security fix that reads as an outage.
- **v2.6.14** (2026-07-26) — **The room knew who could speak but not who had been spoken to (Constellation v2.4.98)** — §13.30.4 answers *who may speak*. Nothing answered *who was spoken to*, and the two are orthogonal — an agent can hold the floor and still not be the one being asked. The failure that gap produces: a human addresses one agent in a three-party room and a second agent answers too, because “a question appeared and I can answer it” was taken for “I was asked”. The floor stops a collision; only addressing stops a misattribution. **§13.30.9** supplies the missing axis. Addressing binds by **declaration, never by resemblance** — the same invariant §13.33.3-6 codified two cuts ago after a seat name substring-matched a peer project’s channel, now applied to a second surface for the same reason: names in a shared room are generic, so similarity matching *fails by succeeding* and yields a confident answer to someone else’s question. The resolution ladder is structured `addressee[]` (or a mention entity carrying an identity object) → `replyTo` → a `@handle` matched **exactly** against a registered alias table → nothing, which is terminal. Identities are registered by each participant and resolution **fails closed**; an ambiguous handle resolves to neither party. The load-bearing rule is the dual of D2: being named creates an obligation, so **not** being named creates the opposite. Three cases that feel like being addressed and are not — a **human** was named (being able to answer is not being asked, and answering anyway takes the exchange away from the person it was handed to); **another agent** was named (not a race — addressing and floor are separate gates and both must clear); your **name inside a body** addressed elsewhere (a third-party reference, which may be a reason to volunteer through a floor bid but never an obligation). Normalization is the **gateway’s** duty, not each recipient’s: a bridge translates native addressing into envelope fields before fan-out, because N recipients interpreting raw text independently will not agree, and the symptom is one silence and one answer to the same message. Measured platform detail that shaped the design: Telegram distinguishes a `text_mention` carrying a `User` object from an `@username` string — one is a declaration, the other needs resolution, which is exactly the ladder’s top two rungs. The **monitoring stance** gives the not-named case a defined posture instead of leaving it per-adapter: participant / monitor / absent, with the monitor carrying no obligation, defaulting to silence, and interjecting only on a named trigger (an error in a domain it owns, a decision resting on a premise it can falsify, a blocking dependency it owns, an explicit invitation) routed through a floor bid that states the trigger. It must not interject to agree, to restate, or to announce that it has been monitoring — the three ways an attentive observer becomes a cost. And a precondition worth stating because it is easy to assume away: on some gateways an agent **cannot** monitor by default — a Telegram bot runs with privacy mode enabled and receives only commands, replies to its own messages, and its own mentions. Lifting that means receiving every message in the group, which is an operator decision with a privacy cost and never the agent’s own call. An agent lacking the capability must **say so**, because a room that believes it has an observer and does not is worse off than a room with none. **§13.32.6** covers the moment before any board exists: an autonomous agent handed the standard should treat reception as *installation, not production* — install the charter, mount the defaults, name what is off, and stop. Building a demonstration is the failure mode, since it produces an unrequested artifact while the charter that would govern how it is recorded is still absent. One rule splits the layer: **default-mount pure discipline; require an explicit request for anything that runs a process, binds a port, spends money, or claims authority.** Discipline is wrong to withhold — an agent that could have avoided a misattribution and waited to be asked is worse for the wait. So skills and conduct mount by default while the board server, peer-join, an organization, release-blocking gates, device notifications and resident loops are opt-in with their cost inside the offer. Conduct therefore binds **before** infrastructure: §13.30.9 is surface-independent and takes effect at three participants in any space — a room, a Telegram group, a bridged channel with no board anywhere — because the misattribution happens on the first multi-party message, long before anyone decides to host a board. Deferring conduct until orchestration exists inverts the order in which the failures occur. Bootstrap also precedes the first deliverable, **including on non-code projects**: the charter decides where decisions are recorded, so work done first leaves its decisions nowhere; research, writing and operations workspaces take the same charter and are the ones most often missing exactly what it supplies. The kit skill carries the procedure (`/eg-bootstrap` §0.0 reception order, §0.1 bootstrap-first, §4a/§4b the split) and `/roundtable` gains D10-D12 as the agent-side duties. No new research run: the multi-party and harness studies already on disk supplied the conventions (mention-as-notification-gate, silence-as-default, when-to-speak self-assessment, the `addressee`/`replyTo`/`floorIntent` schema fields shipped in §13.30.3). What they did not supply was the mechanism — ingestion, self-attribution, alias resolution, lurker stance — and that is design, not fact-finding. One narrow verification was done rather than assumed, because the spec states it normatively: Telegram’s two mention entity kinds and its default privacy mode.
- **v2.6.13** (2026-07-26) — **Recorded is not surfaced: 17 utterances sat in an inbox having never woken anyone (Constellation v2.4.97)** — v2.6.12 closed the case where an untargeted utterance never reaches the main agent. Replaying this deployment’s accumulated inbox through the new coalescer exposed a second silence on the path where it *does* arrive — and this one had been running the whole time. **51 external text frames → 17 utterances, 3,470 characters, zero wakes, ever.** A **targeted** text stream is relayed and written to the inbox faithfully; but `TEXT_MESSAGE_*` frames carry no `name`, and every consumer that gates on `name` — the wake filter, the §13.16.9 meaningful-inbound allowlist, the MCP meaningful set — dropped them without a word. Four of the seventeen were substantive (a contract-status confirmation, a routing-hardening verification, a cross-track status report); the operator had relayed each one by hand after noticing it on the dashboard, which is exactly the manual step this whole line of work exists to remove. Nothing was lost permanently and there is no backlog to work — the value is prospective. The lesson is the one the measurement names: **a name-gated pipeline turns a missing field into silence rather than an error.** So §13.13.3(e) makes the coalesced record a *named* envelope and requires `AgentText` registered in every name-gated consumer, on the same rule any new declaration event follows — producer and consumer filters ship in one cut, or the producer ships alone and nothing changes. This cut is the consumer half v2.6.12 should have carried: it was shipped a producer short, which is the exact lapse the rule exists to prevent. The two live bridges are a **parallel implementation**, not a copy of the reference one, so a fix to the reference reaches neither. Rather than hand-porting the logic twice — which starts the drift on the same day, invisibly — the coalescing semantics now live in one shared module both require, the same move already made for glob semantics. Verified by replay against real accumulated traffic rather than only against frames of my own construction: a synthetic smoke shows the contract holds, a replay shows what was actually being lost. Also calibrated, since the same replay measures it: **13 of the 17 were the peer’s own lifecycle chatter** rendered as text (*interrupting*, *working — 18 min*, *deduped a redelivery*, *watchdog draining*). A content-shaped classifier would be the wrong answer — fragile, and the volume is roughly eight utterances a month, so the noise costs less than the machinery. The structural fix belongs to the sender and already exists: status has names, and anything load-bearing should be an addressed `CUSTOM`.
- **v2.6.12** (2026-07-26) — **An utterance with no addressee still has a recipient, and none was listening (Constellation v2.4.96)** — A collaborating agent that simply *speaks* on a live board — a `TEXT_MESSAGE_*` stream with no `targetAgentId`, which is what an adapter emits when its author thinks of the board as a room rather than a mailbox — reached the boards and the history store and stopped there. The main agent’s inbox never saw it. Nothing errored, and the dashboard was correct precisely because it was the only consumer receiving the frames. Measured twice; the worse instance cost six hours, during which a peer’s substantive replies sat on screen until the operator said “check it”. **§13.13.3** gives the lane a recipient rule, as two halves that only work together: the server extends its target-unspecified fallback from `CUSTOM` to text frames, and the bridge — which returned on every non-`CUSTOM` frame — records them. **Gated on the sender’s declared role, not on frame shape.** The naive version re-creates a defect already paid for: a `local` sender is our own side, whose mirrors emit the identical frames continuously, and routing those to main is the false-wake cascade fixed in July with a `CUSTOM`-only guard on the worker’s poller — a guard this cut deliberately leaves in place. Frame shape cannot tell an utterance from an echo; only the declared identity of the sender can, which is §13.33.3-6 again: bind on what a party declared itself to be, never on what a payload resembles. The bridge coalesces the three frames into **one** record rather than relaying fragments — an agent left to reassemble a delta stream has been handed the bridge’s job, and one wake per fragment triples the cost of the very path being fixed. A `CONTENT` frame with no preceding `START` lands as `partial` instead of being dropped, a whitespace-only utterance is not recorded, and the buffer is bounded so a lost `END` cannot leak an entry for the process’s lifetime. Verified end to end against an isolated server on its own port with the real bridge, a keyed external party and an unkeyed local one — then verified in the other direction, against staged copies with the fix reverted, where it fails 7 of 11. Three of those failures are absence claims the first negative run passed **vacuously**: with nothing recorded at all, “the empty utterance was not recorded” and “the local sender’s text did not arrive” are trivially true, and the zero measures the instrument rather than the behaviour — the trap Corporate §8.2 names. Each is now gated on recording having happened and reports VACUOUS when it has not. Also fixes this project’s own release surface, found by the same round: README’s **Current** marker had been number-bumped across eleven cuts while its body stayed frozen on v2.6.5’s summary, and the Previously chain skipped the entire v2.6 line. A number-only check passes a frozen body, so the version-sync axis now compares the Current summary against the changelog entry for that version, not just the version string.
- **v2.6.11** (2026-07-26) — **Whether a model can staff a seat is decided by the harness, and one of ours could not be staffed at all (Corporate v0.1.9)** — A survey of custom-endpoint reach across the three measured CLIs turned a model-assignment question into a harness question, and the registry gains a `providerBind` row per harness: one accepts arbitrary OpenAI-compatible endpoints through a declared provider but only over the Responses wire (chat/completions was deprecated 2026-02 and a provider declaring it now fails at startup), one accepts its vendor plus three named clouds and nothing else, and one exposes no provider surface at all. So holding an API key is never by itself an assignment — the reachable-seat set can be empty. Two findings generalize into §9.3. **An endpoint is not a harness**: a seat needs something that *calls* a model, and this deployment had one seat whose harness field held a URL — unstaffable, and healthy-looking because every other field was well-formed. The roster check that had been passing it was the defect, so it now rejects a harness resolving to a URL, and it failed on the seat immediately; the seat is redeclared on the CLI that ships a local provider. **A provider choice can be scoped above the seat**: one CLI honors provider selection only at user scope and ignores a project-local override with a startup warning, so a per-seat provider cannot live in the desk and the mechanism becomes a per-invocation profile — otherwise the assignment sits in the chart while the process runs the user default. Separately, the chart emitter stopped defaulting an unknown seat status to `idle`: re-emitting the chart had silently overwritten a working seat as idle, which is invariant 1 violated by the *writer* rather than the reader. NVIDIA’s free API is recorded on the watchlist as **not** a candidate for any resident seat — ~40 RPM, a ~5k-call credit budget, a wire that may not reach the one harness accepting custom providers, and public sources that contradict each other on whether the free tier trains on submitted content, which §9.1 makes the operator’s call rather than an inference.
- **v2.6.10** (2026-07-26) — **A round loop, specified by how it stops (Constellation v2.4.95)** — Repeating a round until the queue stops yielding is easy to write and easy to get wrong in one specific way: the round’s own new-work scan can always find something to write down, so a loop that counts registration as progress runs forever and reports a growing backlog as momentum. §13.34 therefore fixes the **productivity predicate** first — a round is productive only if it started work or cleared a blocker, and registering planned items, re-sorting, refreshing a `blockReason` or filing a gate are explicitly not progress. Under that rule a loop that only writes things down is exhausted by definition, which is the correct reading. Six termination conditions are declared **before** the first round rather than discovered mid-run (dry-round threshold, a remainder that is no longer self-actionable, caps, a stall detected by state measurement rather than by the round’s own claim, context pressure, and an interrupt that takes effect at a round boundary so the board is never half-written), and a loop that stops without naming which one fired is indistinguishable from a crash. One rule exists only because loops have it and hand-run rounds do not: **a round completes when its board write is measured, not when it is sent** — reading the next round’s ripeness before the previous write lands re-starts work already running, which is the same ack-is-not-processing window §13.13 documents. Repetition grants no authority: the loop cannot resolve a gate, widen its own caps, or decide a human-gated fork because that fork is all that is left. Ships as the `/roundloop` skill; the product of a run is the list of decisions only a human can make, not the round count.
- **v2.6.9** (2026-07-26) — **The organization’s vocabulary becomes entries, and the wiki tab stops serving a stale copy of them (Constellation v2.4.94)** — Corporate §8.4 said role terms belong in the vocabulary substrate where one is present. Seven now are — durable role, desk, locker, charter, residency class, roster, liaison — promoted on measured usage (word-boundary counts over the spec corpus; substring counting would have inflated `locker` from 26 to 463 by matching inside *blocker*, which is the same trap v2.6.6 fixed in the seat resolver). Writing them was itself a dogfood: the store’s own pointer-not-paraphrase lint rejected all seven for carrying definitions over its 300-character cap, which is exactly the discipline the module exists to enforce, applied to its author. Rewritten as one-line glosses plus a pointer, they pass with 34 entries and zero warnings. The org chart now links a seat’s terms to their entries — and only where the entry exists, since a link to a missing entry is the same false affordance the previous cuts removed. **The load-bearing find is the projection itself**: the wiki tab fetches a derived `compendium.json` that was being copied by hand, so it had been serving 27 entries from six days earlier while the store held 34 — a tab that looked healthy precisely because nothing signals a stale derivation. It now rides the dashboard deploy path.
- **v2.6.8** (2026-07-26) — **The practice-to-seat derivation becomes a computation, and running it found an unowned surface (Corporate v0.1.8)** — §8.2 claimed that a codified practice is evidence a seat is warranted, and §8.3 claimed the same signal inverted is an eviction trigger. Both were prose. Implementing them turned up two failure modes the prose did not anticipate, and both are now specified. **Provenance is not target**: a practice entry cites the research it rests on and the sibling entries it rolls up as well as the surface it governs, and attributing on all of them collapses every practice onto the practice store itself — on this repo’s store 26 of 30 entries resolved to `greatpractice/` and `reports/` until the evidence blocks and store-internal paths were excluded. **A seat with no declared boundary cannot be measured either way**: coordination seats own no files by design, so their zero measures the instrument, and a test that cannot produce a positive must not be read as a negative — the honest output is *unmeasurable*, named as such, which also means the eviction window for a staffed seat starts at staffing rather than at declaration. With both corrections the derivation ran against this project and produced a real finding: five practices govern the documentation and version surfaces (`docs/`, `README.md`) and **no seat owns those paths** — the publication work that every release cut performs has no responsible seat, which is exactly the class of gap §8.2 exists to surface. Recorded as a proposal rather than acted on, because seat creation is a human call.
- **v2.6.7** (2026-07-26) — **A seat stops reporting itself busy after its session ends (Constellation v2.4.93 · Corporate v0.1.7)** — `RoleState` is persisted and replayed like any latest-wins declaration, but what it asserts is a seat’s condition *at the moment a live process said so*. Nothing expired it, so the org chart kept rendering `working` from a session that had ended — and the cut that put the board on machine start made that the **default** view: a board opening the morning to an empty house, reporting work in progress. Now a status renders as declared only while the seat’s own agent is present (§13.9.4); otherwise it folds to unknown **with the reason named**, and the last value survives in the detail view labelled last-known rather than in the node as current. Three details are load-bearing and each is a way of not lying: it folds to *unknown* and never to `offline`, because `offline` is a value an agent declares about itself and inferring it manufactures a declaration (invariant 2); liveness anchors to the seat’s own `agentId` rather than to whoever declared on its behalf, so a main going down does not make the scribe’s state stale; and a seat with no declared `agentId` has no liveness anchor at all, so the fallback is a stated time horizon rather than indefinite trust. Quoting the stale value is not the problem — presenting it as current is, so the card names it and denies it in the same breath. Captured as `Constellation.md §13.33.3` invariant 7 (invariant 1’s dual) and `Corporate.md §10.2`. The talk affordance also moves to each card’s top-right corner, so the button sits on one line across cards of different heights. Browser-measured: 8 freshness assertions (including that the declaration data itself is preserved and only the rendering folds) plus the 10 existing affordance assertions.
- **v2.6.6** (2026-07-26) — **The org chart’s talk affordance binds by declaration, not by resemblance (Constellation v2.4.92 · Corporate v0.1.6)** — A seat’s talk button opened another project’s main. Two defects stacked. First, the fallback that runs when a seat declares no `agentId` matched by **substring** over channel ids and names, and seat names are generic organizational nouns — `main` matched a peer project’s `…-main` channel, so the affordance did not fail, it *succeeded against the wrong organization*, with only a soft note calling the match approximate. Second, the authoritative path added one cut earlier returned a bare id string where every consumer expected `{id, exact}`, so for the two seats that *do* declare an agent the switch silently no-op’d and the realtime window opened on whichever channel happened to be active — again a peer channel. To the operator the two failure modes were indistinguishable, and both looked like success. Now a declared `agentId` is the only binding and is fail-closed; the nameless fallback is exact-equality only, over local-side identities (`peer`/`upstream`/`collab` are never candidates, because a seat belongs to *this* organization by construction); and an affordance with nothing to bind renders visibly unbound and opens nothing, since landing on an unrelated channel is worse than refusing. The reason is written into the row text rather than a tooltip — passing `null` let the row renderer fold *declared-but-not-joined* and *never-declared* into one word, which is the §13.31.1 render-default failure one layer up. Captured as `Constellation.md §13.33.3` invariant 6 (MUST) and as a bound on `Corporate.md §10.1`, whose fallback permission had explicitly allowed the heuristic that caused this. Verified in a browser against the live board: 13 assertions, including that no seat resolves to a peer, upstream, or collab channel.
- **v2.6.5** (2026-07-26) — **The required-field table stops contradicting the section it points at (Corporate v0.1.5)** — A one-line internal contradiction, fixed rather than left to be discovered by whoever pastes it into a validator. §10.1's required-field table listed `lane` as `interactive | automation` while §9.1 — rewritten two cuts earlier — documents **three** lanes, the third being `local` for an endpoint on the operator's own machine. The deployment's own roster already uses it: the release-surveillance seat runs on a locally-served model precisely because that lane raises no entitlement question and costs nothing per wake. So the table was the stale surface, not the prose, and a validator built from the table would have rejected a seat the spec elsewhere recommends. The row now carries all three values and states the actual requirement plainly — what is mandatory is the declaration plus a one-line rationale, not any particular value, which is the §9.1 position the table was contradicting. Found by a scheduling round's own new-work scan rather than by a consumer hitting it.
- **v2.6.4** (2026-07-25) — **The board renders the organization (Constellation v2.4.91 · Corporate v0.1.4)** — The org chart is no longer a contract on paper: the board renders it. A new **조직도 tab** sits between the decisions panel and the wiki, and it is fed by the two declaration events §13.33 defined a cut ago — so an organization whose roster is local and gitignored now reaches a board that hosts none of it. Built as four write-disjoint lanes behind a frozen contract (wire · markup+styles · render+wiring · declaration script), then put through a consistency gate that checked ten axes by grep rather than by impression — and the gate earned its place by **refuting one lane's own self-report** (a push guard claimed at two call sites existed at one). **The invariant that mattered held, and was measured**: seven unstaffed seats render as *unknown* with a 미선언 label, not as idle. A browser run against the live board confirms it — chart-internal counts of `unknown=7`, `working=1`, `idle=1` against exactly two declared states, zero uncaught runtime errors, the detail popup opening with honest "선언되지 않았어요" sections where data is absent rather than plausible defaults, and the mobile bottom bar highlighting correctly (a pre-existing gap the wiki tab shared, fixed here for both). **One root cause fixed rather than approximated**: seat↔agent matching was being guessed from name similarity in *two* places, and seat names legitimately do not resemble agent ids — a `scribe` seat filled by a `board-observer` process matches nothing, so the talk affordance the tab exists to provide would have silently done nothing. `agentId` is now an optional role field that is **authoritative and fail-closed where declared** (a mismatch refuses rather than falling back to similarity) and absent on unstaffed seats, because that absence is information. Three cross-file surfaces the lanes correctly declined to touch were closed afterwards: the canonical Web Push noise list, the worker's pending classifier (without which the scribe would have misread an org declaration as work to do), and room-participant object forms that the server's string normaliser had been silently dropping — the class of defect that renders fine live and vanishes after a restart. Deployed end to end: dashboard synced, server copied, board restarted with no record loss, chart and states persisted, History payload carrying both fields. verify-nway 23-axis PASS.
- **v2.6.3** (2026-07-25) — **The registry becomes a measurement (Corporate v0.1.3)** — The registry stopped being a reading of documentation and became a measurement. Every harness in it was installed on the deployment host, so v2.6.3 ran them and recorded what the binaries actually say. **Three `agy` gaps closed**: the full flag table exists (nineteen flags, nine subcommands), `--print-timeout` really does default to 5m0s, and the `-c` ambiguity resolves in favour of the documentation — `-c` is the alias of `--continue`, with `--conversation <id>` separate. Two findings that change how a seat is placed there: `--effort` offers only `low|medium|high`, and **print mode has no JSON or output-format option at all** — it emits prose.
